Anesthesiologists should be careful to reduce the severity and duration of hypotension during arterial pressure monitoring as it increases the risk of organ damage, complications, length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital, mortality and morbidity, and cost.[ ] If hypertension is not treated, it increases the risk of organ damage, primarily CVS complications (35%), left ventricular failure, myocardial infarction, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury (AKI), and intracranial bleeding. Therefore, it is extremely important to prevent, diagnose, and treat hypotension and hypertension early.[ ] In patients with low CO and inadequate tissue perfusion, all vital parameters should be evaluated according to CO or cardiac index (CI), even if BP is within normal limits.[ ] Hypotension may cause an imbalance between oxygen supply and demand because it disrupts the perfusion of vital organs.[ ] Hypotension, as a symptom of macrocirculation, may not provide sufficient information about microcirculation. Ineffective use of O 2 due to inadequate tissue perfusion or blood flow distribution causes cellular defects that may lead to microcirculation disorders even if macrocirculation initially appears adequate.[ ] When MAP remains below 55 mmHg for 1–5 min, the risk of organ damage becomes more apparent [ ].[ ] The most common cause of hypotension during anesthesia, especially in the first 20 min, is the excessive depth of anesthesia. As hypotension develops due to the vasodilator effects of anesthetic drugs, it is more appropriate to reduce the anesthetic drugs in order, then replace fluids, and start vasopressors early if necessary. Other causes include advanced age (>65 years), preoperative hypovolemia, ASA status, taking antihypertension and diuretic drugs, obesity, ejection fraction (EF) <40%, positive pressure for mechanical ventilation, regional anesthesia, pregnancy, patients on dialysis, intraoperative hypothermia, hypoxemia, and hypovolemia due to bleeding.[ ] Especially in patients over 65 years of age who use angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and ARBs in the preoperative period, these drugs should be stopped 24 h before the operation and started 48 h after the operation.[ ] Profound hypotension can increase end-organ damage, especially in the heart, kidneys, and brain. Therefore, it is important to keep MAP above 65 mmHg to prevent end-organ damage.[ ] Causes of hypertension in the perioperative period are frequently uncontrolled and undiagnosed hypertension, age >65 years, obesity, preeclampsia, stopping of medications, stress/anxiety, inadequate premedication and anesthesia/analgesia, airway/surgery stimulation, hypoxemia and hypercarbia, hypervolemia, hypothermia, ketamine, metabolic diseases, laparoscopic surgery, and urinary retention. Therefore, providing organ perfusion and preventing end-organ damage is important.[ ] Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is closely related to MAP in the intraoperative period. MAP should be kept between 50 and 150 mmHg. CPP = MAP − ICP (intracranial pressure). The average value for CPP is between 70 and 80 mmHg. When MAP or CPP increases, resistance in small cerebral arteries increases, leading to vasoconstriction. Conversely, when MAP (<50 mmHg) or CPP decreases, it causes vasodilation. The cerebral autoregulation mechanism is an important mechanism that physiologically involves myogenic, neurogenic, metabolic, and humoral factors in regulating BP. The main purpose of this autoregulation mechanism is to provide oxygenation, optimize cerebral perfusion, provide blood flow to the organs, and reduce end-organ damage. It is especially important to provide perfusion in hypertension, chronic kidney failure, diabetes mellitus, and cerebrovascular diseases.[ ] When the limit values of MAP 50–150 mmHg are exceeded due to dysautoregulation, oxygenation is impaired, and organ damage occurs. The kidney, brain, and heart are quite compatible with this. Therefore, it is essential to avoid sudden BP changes to maintain cerebral perfusion.[ ] Therefore, keeping the patient’s BP within normal limits throughout the perioperative period is one of the primary responsibilities of the knowledgeable, trained, and guideline-based anesthesiologist, and BP optimization is extremely important for quality and positive outcomes. Volume status Detailed assessment of the patient’s volume status during the perioperative period is crucial. It is a challenging goal for an anesthesiologist to provide effective intravenous volume, maintain fluid-electrolyte homeostasis and normovolemia, adequate hemodynamic stability, and tissue perfusion and oxygenation. Both hypovolemia and hypervolemia are associated with potentially increased adverse outcomes.[ ] Regardless of the type of anesthesia and surgery performed, our primary goal should be to maintain the patient in a normovolemic state by administering the right fluid at the right time, volume, and rate according to the patient’s needs, taking into account the current intraoperative clinical status and other risk factors. Hypotension due to vasodilation caused by induction of general and/or neuraxial anesthesia, hypotension resulting from positive pressure ventilation, and volume/blood loss can be corrected with intravenous volume replacement. In patients with comorbidities, a vasopressor should be started early to prevent hypervolemia and avoid excessive volume administration, if necessary, to reduce vasodilation and increase the fluid responsiveness of vascular tone.[ ] Fluid maintenance should be performed according to the Frank-Starling law, considering the patient’s basic needs and losses from the skin, UO, airways, and surgical field.[ ] Whereas a hypovolemic state is associated with hypotension, hypoperfusion, hypoxemia, inflammation, lactatemia, lactic acidosis, and organ dysfunction, hypervolemia is associated with increased cell, tissue, and organ edema; inflammation; acidosis; and coagulopathy [ ].[ ] Hypervolemia contributes to fluid retention in the interstitial space by increasing intravascular hydrostatic pressure, causing fluid to shift from circulation to the interstitium by damaging the endothelial glycocalyx, which provides vascular permeability. The resulting interstitial edema can lead to intestinal wall edema and prolonged postoperative ileus. The increase in these complications leads to lengthy hospital stays and increased hospital costs. In anesthesia, individualized fluid management is more appropriate, considering the patient’s current comorbidities and the surgery’s type, duration, and complexity.[ ] “Enhanced recovery after surgery” (ERAS) protocols include correct and appropriate patient fluid management in the perioperative period and are essential in reducing postoperative mortality and morbidity.[ ] According to the patient’s condition, minimally invasive methods (HR, BP, SpO 2 ) should be considered first to optimize perioperative hemodynamics and manage the patient correctly. If necessary, bedside transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and lung ultrasound (US) should be performed according to the patient’s current comorbidities and the type and risk of surgery. To correctly assess volume status, several advanced hemodynamic monitoring parameters are essential. These include central venous catheterization and cardiac output (CO) monitoring, as well as stroke volume variation (SVV), pulse pressure variation (PPV), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), cardiac index (CI), central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO 2 ), extravascular lung water (EVLW), and mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO 2 ). These parameters play a critical role in guiding intraoperative management, particularly in major surgeries where fluid shifts are significant and the risks of bleeding and hypovolemia are high.[ ] In light of this information, optimizing the patient’s volume status that affects the prognosis will be shaped according to the anesthesiologist’s clinical knowledge, attitude, behavior, and experience. Oxygen Ensuring adequate oxygen delivery to the patient’s tissues and organs in the perioperative period and maintaining the balance between adequate oxygen delivery (DO 2 ) and consumption (VO 2 ) is of critical importance in anesthesia and surgery in the perioperative period [ ].[ ] Hypoxemia is defined by <60 mmHg (8 kPa) PaO 2 or <90% peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ). It is related to impaired oxygen passage from the blood to the cells, causing damage.[ ] Management of intraoperative hypoxemia during anesthesia remains a significant challenge for anesthesiologists, as the pathophysiology of hypoxemia is quite complex. There are generally five leading causes in the pathophysiology of hypoxemia: decreased fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO 2 ), hypoventilation, ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, diffusion disorder, and shunt.[ ] Close monitoring of SaO 2 (where SaO 2 is the percentage of oxyhemoglobin saturation in arterial blood) and end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO 2 , in which elevated levels may indicate hypoventilation) perioperatively is essential to determine hypoxemia, and their changes must be evaluated in detail. The most common cause of hypoxemia during general anesthesia is V/Q mismatch.[ ] The most common causes of V/Q mismatch are increased dead space, low CO and BP, atelectasis, and hypoventilation. Correction of CO, BP, and pulmonary perfusion; recruitment maneuvers; and reduction of dead space are the main treatment options. The primary goal of safe anesthesia should be to provide ventilation, perfusion, oxygenation, and prevention of hypoxemia.[ ] The balance between DO 2 and VO 2 is crucial for adequate tissue perfusion. In awake, healthy people, at rest, normal DO 2 is 1000 mL min −1 , and VO 2 is 250 mL min −1 [ ].

In awake, healthy people, at rest, normal DO 2 is 1000 mL min −1 , and VO 2 is 250 mL min −1 [ ]. A target DO 2 of 330 or 500 mL min −1 has been suggested to prevent tissue oxygen deficiency under anesthesia.[ ] Under normal physiological conditions, only approximately 20%–30% of the oxygen delivered to the tissues is extracted for metabolic needs. This relationship, referred to as the oxygen extraction ratio (O 2 ER), is defined as the ratio of oxygen consumption (VO 2 ) to oxygen delivery (DO 2 ) and typically ranges between 0.2 and 0.3. If the O 2 ER reaches 0.6–0.8, it is considered maximal—the critical point where VO 2 is DO 2 dependent [ ].[ ] If this vital DO 2 continues to fall below or if VO 2 continues to increase for a given DO 2 critical value, anaerobic respiration begins and results in hyperlactatemia with the development of tissue hypoxia. Subsequently, intracellular acidosis and cell death occur together with mitochondrial dysfunction. Therefore, it is vital to maintain the DO 2 /VO 2 balance under anesthesia.[ ] Anesthesiologists use oxygen at high concentrations as a safety strategy in preoxygenation or before extubation, and as a result, it can put the patient into hyperoxemia. Anesthetists should take a sensible approach to oxygen administration to avoid hyperoxia. Application of perioperative oxygen values to a target PaO 2 of 8–10 kPa or SaO 2 of 88%–92% should be given priority. The FiO 2 is usually titrated to SpO 2 as measured by pulse oximetry, which detects hypoxemia (PaO 2 = 100–200 mmHg) but fails to detect hyperoxemia. The adverse effects of both hyperoxemia and hypoxemia are shown in .[ ] The oxygen reserve index (ORI) is a new continuous, non-invasive parameter based on pulse oximetry. The ORI reflects oxygenation in the moderately hyperoxic range (PaO 2 100–200 mmHg). ORI can provide an early alarm before SpO 2 when oxygenation deteriorates and can prevent unwanted hyperoxia.[ ] In addition to SpO 2 and PaO 2 , ORI and regional cerebral oxygenation (rScO 2 ) are used to detect both hypoxemia and hyperoxemia. rScO 2 monitoring with near-infrared spectroscopy is essential in detecting cerebral hypoperfusion and dysfunction early and can be used to prevent postoperative neurological complications.[ ] None of the available parameters alone is ideal for assessing adequate tissue oxygenation. Therefore, decisions to determine oxygenation should be based on a combined assessment of clinical, oxygenation, and biochemical parameters.[ ] Both hypoxemia and hyperoxemia are associated with increased mortality, morbidity, increased length of ICU and hospital stay, and higher costs. Therefore, a conservative approach to oxygen therapy, aiming to optimize oxygen pressure at physiologic levels according to the patient’s age and existing comorbidities, should be considered the most logical option.[ ] Carbon dioxide The arterial partial pressure of CO 2 in the blood (PaCO 2 ) indicates the balance between produced CO 2 , excreted CO 2, and exhaled CO 2 (rarely). PaCO 2 is determined by minute ventilation, tissue CO 2 production, and the tidal volume fraction from dead space. PaCO 2 , an essential ventilation index, is a valuable indicator of the clinical status of the respiratory system, metabolic system, and CVS. PaCO 2 is essential for determining ventilation adequacy, adjusting machine settings during MV, and identifying and differentiating acid-base, metabolic disorders, and shock states.[ ] The normal range of PaCO 2 is 36–45 mmHg (4.8–6.0 kPa). Anesthesiologists consider PaCO 2 < 36 mmHg hypocapnia and PaCO 2 >45 mmHg hypercapnia, and evaluate the patient’s clinical condition accordingly. The end-tidal CO 2 (EtCO 2 ) indicates minute ventilation during general anesthesia. P(a-Et)CO 2 in healthy awake humans is about 3.6–4.6 mmHg. It can give us valuable information about ventilation and perfusion during anesthesia.[ ] Changes in PaCO 2 and pH cause a shift in the hemoglobin-O 2 dissociation curve (Bohr effect). Higher PaCO 2 and decreased pH allow hemoglobin to bind poorly to oxygen and facilitate the release of O 2 in the periphery. Conversely, lower PaCO 2 and increased pH provide strong binding of hemoglobin to oxygen and make it harder to release O 2 in the periphery. With these changes, V/Q is protected by the lungs and renal mechanisms in the patient.[ ] Hypercarbia causes increased cerebral blood flow (CBF) and ICP due to cerebral vasodilation.

In normotension, the relationship between PaCO 2 and CBF is almost linear to the maximum level of PaCO 2 to 10.6 kPa (80 mmHg). CBF is almost doubled at this point, and no further increase is possible as the arterioles are maximally dilated. In addition to these effects, hypercarbia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, V/Q mismatch, increased pulmonary arterio-venous shunt, and impaired diffusion. In addition, hypermetabolic conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, extrapulmonary causes that reduce chest wall compliance, fever, sepsis, burns, sedatives, neuromuscular diseases, long-term use of CO 2 adsorbent, and excessive carbohydrate-rich diet may cause hypercarbia during anesthesia.[ ] In extreme hypercarbia, where PaCO 2 exceeds 100 mmHg and pH falls below 7, a three-fold increase in VO 2 and a 15- to 20-fold increase in blood lactate can be detected. Tachycardia and arrhythmias may develop clinically due to sympathetic catecholamine fluctuation. These conditions must be considered during anesthesia, and preventive strategies and treatments should be applied.[ ] Hyperventilation reduces PaCO 2 (<4.6 kPa = 35 mmHg hypocarbia) and causes vasoconstriction of cerebral vessels, decreasing CBF and ICP. If PaCO 2 decreases to 2.7 kPa (20 mmHg), the CBF is almost divided equally, and the arterioles are maximally vasoconstricted. This extent of decrease may cause cerebral ischemia. In addition, hypocarbia may cause increased airway pressures, pulmonary vasodilation, cellular dysfunction, deterioration of oxygen supply-demand balance, arrhythmia due to sympathetic discharge, hemodynamic instability, and myocardial changes. These effects of hypocapnia have been shown to increase postoperative mortality and morbidity during anesthesia.[ ] It should be remembered that it is important to maintain normocapnia during anesthesia to maintain CBF, CPP, cerebral vascular resistance, CO, BP, tissue oxygenation, and perfusion. In this context, it is recommended that anesthesiologists have a comprehensive knowledge of the physiological effects of CO 2 and evaluate them according to the existing comorbidities and clinical condition of their patients.[ ] Hypercarbia and increased intra-abdominal pressure due to pneumoperitoneum applied in laparoscopic surgery and the resulting sympathetic discharge effect cause physiological changes, especially in the respiratory system and CVS, and the patient’s position changes. In addition to the direct effects of gas insufflation on the patient, it can cause more serious consequences, especially in those with morbidity or obesity and the elderly.[ ] For this reason, in anesthesiology and ICU practice, a suitable ventilator strategy should be applied to the patient by considering the existing etiological factors in terms of both hypercarbia and hypocarbia. Despite all the adverse effects, anesthesiologists have difficulty solving this problem. The average core temperature in healthy individuals is 36.5°C–37.3°C. Hypothermia is defined as BT < 36°C. It is thought that 70%–90% of patients undergoing surgery develop hypothermia, even after 1 h of surgery. Hypothermia during anesthesia results from impaired thermoregulation. Thermoregulation occurs in three phases: afferent pathways, thermal sensing, and central regulation. The principle of thermoregulation depends on the balance between heat loss and heat production. Efferent responses are produced by CT, metabolism, and muscle movements and are regulated by autonomic feedback mechanisms from the anterior hypothalamus. The primary mechanism of hypothermia in anesthesia results from internal heat redistribution. These events occur in phases I, II, and III. Therefore, keeping the patient in normothermia is essential for reducing perioperative complications [ ].[ ] Urine output Stress during anesthesia and surgery can affect kidney function and fluid regulation. The release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in the perioperative period is a natural response to stress factors; thus, a decrease in UO may occur during and after major surgery. With its direct effects depending on the type and dose of the agent used in anesthesia, changes in the ADH effect may also cause changes in the autoregulation of renal blood flow (RBF).[ ] The kidneys receive 20% of the CO, which means 1200 mL of blood circulates through the kidneys each minute. Most anesthetic and adjuvant drugs cause dose-dependent vasodilation and myocardial depression that may lead to hypotension. Renal autoregulation is regulated by RBF and renal perfusion pressure (RPP). The MAP for this autoregulation is between 50 and 150 mmHg. With a value below 80 mmHg, RBF and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) decrease. Along with hypotension induced by anesthetic drugs, the risk of developing perioperative AKI increases due to impaired renal autoregulation. It is quite significant to keep the MA P value >65 mmHg to prevent the progression of AKI.[ ] Perioperative causes of oliguria as a physiological response may be due to intravascular hypovolemia, prolonged hypotension, and renal hypoperfusion, as well as non-renal conditions that cause the release of ADH, such as in response to nausea or pain.[ ] Although the effects of regional anesthesia are less visible than general anesthesia, they are mostly related to changes in systemic hemodynamics. Sympathetic blockade during neuraxial anesthesia can result in relative hypovolemia due to increased venous capacitance and dilation of arteriolar resistance vessels, with resistance hypotension.[ ] Rather than preloading with intravenous fluid, a traditional practice, using a vasopressor such as phenylephrine or norepinephrine, is preferred. Inhalational anesthetics, barbiturates, opioids, and benzodiazepines also generally decrease GFR and UO. Avoiding unnecessarily deep anesthesia avoids hypotension and related unnecessary fluid administration. Hypotension that persists despite the reduction in anesthetic depth (if appropriate) and fluid administration to replace known surgical losses can be treated with intravenous vasopressor/inotropic agents such as phenylephrine.[ ] AKI accounts for 20% of all hospitalizations. Therefore, UO should be considered an important parameter to be monitored in the perioperative period.[ ] Hemoglobin Oxygen in the atmosphere enters the respiratory tract, passes into the alveoli, and diffuses from the alveoli to the pulmonary blood.[ ] The link between oxygen and hemoglobin is crucial in managing patients under anesthesia, critical illness, and resuscitation. The amount of dissolved O 2 , the hemoglobin level in the blood, and the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen determine the oxygen level in the blood. Hemoglobin is the predominant protein in the blood, and hemoglobin acts as a carrier of oxygen, CO 2 , and some nitric oxide (NO). The balance of gas exchange between the capillary system and the alveoli maintains normal cardiopulmonary homeostasis.[ ] According to the World Health Organization (WHO), anemia is a hemoglobin level below 12 g/dL in women and below 13 g/dL in men. The primary physiologic consequence of severe anemia to the surgical patient is inadequate tissue DO 2 , which may lead to tissue hypoxia, biochemical imbalances, organ dysfunction, and ultimately organ damage. Anemia is a common blood disorder in perioperative patients and significantly increases the risk of perioperative complications and transfusion and raises the risk of mortality and morbidity. In the perioperative period, inflammation, surgical blood loss, nutritional deficiencies, iron deficiency, and underlying chronic disorders are the most critical factors contributing to anemia.[ ] Decreased hemoglobin concentration reduces the DO 2 capacity of the blood. Various mechanisms exist to reduce anemia’s effect and compensate for the reduction of DO 2 in tissues. Decreased DO 2 activates the stabilizing mechanisms at the subcellular level, mainly via the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling pathway. The hemoglobin-O 2 dissociation curve, related to the percentage saturation of the oxygen-carrying power of Hb to PaO 2 , has a characteristic sigmoid shape. The oxygen dissociation curve of hemoglobin is shifted to the right following lower pH, increased accumulation of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), and other NO-mediated signaling events that facilitate oxygen release and increase the hemoglobin oxygen extraction rate. It is essential to know the differences between the variables of DO 2 and VO 2 in anemia, as these may lead to hypoxemia.[ ] Compensatory changes develop in CO and SaO 2 saturation to prevent hypoxemia. In anemia, there is a decrease in blood viscosity, thus reducing SVR and increasing CO. Sympathetic activation by stimulating chemoreceptors due to hypoxemia may also contribute to this situation. CO is also redistributed to organs with high oxygen demand, such as the brain and heart.[ ] Our general approach should avoid transfusion by applying preventive strategies as much as possible and monitoring the patient correctly in the perioperative period. Detection of anemia in the preoperative period is critical in terms of optimization. Optimizing anemia preoperatively results in higher Hb concentrations and less transfusion need. Perioperative hyperglycemia is related to increased complications risk in diabetic and nondiabetic patients. Therefore, these deficiencies should be corrected.[ ] High HbA 1 C levels and hyperglycemia are associated with adverse outcomes. The optimal perioperative evaluation of patients with DM should include screening patients at risk for hyperglycemia and preoperative use of oral hypoglycemics and insulin. The type of anesthetic method and drugs, tight blood glucose (BG) monitoring, and treatment for hyperglycemia that will develop during surgery should be considered perioperatively. In general, it is routine practice to discontinue all oral antihyperglycemic drugs on the day of surgery. The recommended perioperative BG goal is <180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L). Tight glycemic control (TGC) is a clinical practice to keep BG in a healthy adult within 80–110 mg/dL (4.4–6.1 mmol/L).[ ] DM type, degree of hyperglycemia and HbA 1 C levels, type and duration of surgery, anesthesia method, the fragility of the patient, immunosuppression, malnutrition, comorbidities, pre and postoperative expected fasting period, and compliance with medical treatment should be evaluated with a multidisciplinary approach. Patients with severe hyperglycemia (BG ≥ 300 mg/dL, 16.6 mmol/L) who will undergo elective surgery should be evaluated comprehensively in the preoperative period. BG measurement is made on the day of surgery, and anesthesia management and BG treatment should be applied accordingly.[ ] Hypoglycemia is BG ≤ 70 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L). Hypoglycemia may be difficult to detect under anesthesia, as symptoms such as tremors, sweating, anxiety, and palpitations cannot be observed. Appropriate monitoring of patients with diabetes is essential to detect hypoglycemia early in the perioperative period.[ ] The type of anesthesia affects BG regulation. Regional methods such as spinal and epidural anesthesia suppress the sympathetic response to surgery. Uncontrolled BG levels, such as hyper or hypoglycemia, can cause sudden hemodynamic changes in consciousness, organ dysfunction, seizures, or neurological injuries.[ ] Both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia should be avoided as they contribute significantly to increased mortality and morbidity in the perioperative duration, prolonged hospital stay, and adverse outcomes.[ ] Osmolarity Systemic osmoregulation is a necessary process that regulates digestive behavior, sympathetic outflow, and renal function to stabilize changes in plasma osmolality, extracellular fluid tonicity, and volume detected through osmoreceptors.[ ] In addition, osmoreceptors affect homeostasis, including fluid-electrolyte balance, thermoregulation, and cardiovascular balance.[ ] Serum osmolarity is generally in the range of 275–295 mOsm/L. Osmotic stability is achieved via changes in sodium and fluid intake. Regulations in fluid balance are made by hypothalamic signals regulating ADH’s thirst and secretion. Changes in fluid homeostasis can disrupt cell structure and function. Therefore, regulating fluid balance is essential for cells, tissues, and organs to function.[ ] Under normal physiological conditions, the osmolarity and sodium balance of extracellular fluids (ECFs) are controlled by two regulatory mechanisms that modulate water balance and sodium output from signals collected via osmoreceptors and baroreceptors, respectively. In addition, isotonicity is on both sides of the blood-brain barrier (BBB). In systemic osmolarity disorders, water transport occurs at the BBB level. However, it does not affect the osmolarity of cerebral ECFs in pathophysiological osmolarity changes such as acute circulating hyponatremia and hypernatremia. An intact BBB acts as a semipermeable membrane that allows water to be transported according to osmotic laws. It creates an osmotic gradient on both sides of the BBB.[ ] However, if it is degraded, it can cause osmotic edema or brain tissue dehydration, depending on the water direction. The normal value of blood sodium level is 135–145 mEq/L. Hyponatremia is blood sodium measurement below 135 mEq/L, and hypernatremia is above 145 mEq/L. The following formula calculates blood osmolarity: Blood osmolarity = (2 × (Na + +K + )) + (BUN/2.8) + (BG/18). Hypo or hyper-natremia may result in volume changes by disrupting the osmotic balance and may result in several clinical manifestations such as confusion, lethargy, weakness, seizures, and even coma.[ ] Rapid correction of electrolyte imbalances, especially sodium, hypovolemia, and hypervolemia, may lead to permanent severe sequelae such as brain edema, convulsions, axonal damage, and demyelination. For this reason, the proper fluid should be administered at the appropriate amount and duration, considering osmolarity during the correction of electrolyte imbalances. Hyper- or hypoglycemia may also lead to sudden changes in osmolarity; therefore, maintenance of normoglycemia should be ensured as far as possible concerning osmolarity.[ ] In the perioperative period, both hypoosmolarity and hyperosmolarity contribute to acute and chronic inflammation, impair BBB, and affect many body functions resulting from osmotic imbalance, leading to volume shifts and, consequently, organ dysfunction and neurological damage. Therefore, both are associated with increased mortality and morbidity.[ ] Lactate Lactate is a product of anaerobic metabolism and is an excellent diagnostic, therapeutic, and prognostic marker of global tissue hypoxia. Lactate exists in two isomers: L-lactate and D-lactate.[ ] Lactate levels rise when production increases and or clearance decreases. In addition, increased lactate may be a response to increased circulating catecholamines, inflammatory cytokine release, or accumulation of leukocytes at the site of inflammation. Regardless of the underlying cause, early detection of hyperlactatemia is very helpful in providing sufficient oxygenation and perfusion to the patient. As hyperlactatemia is associated with an increased risk of mortality and morbidity, it requires a comprehensive, rapid, and systematic approach to diagnosis and management.[ ] The etiology of high lactate levels includes hypoperfusion, hypotension, hypovolemia, liver dysfunction, mitochondrial dysfunction, hypermetabolic conditions, infection, sepsis, and shock.[ ] The normal value of plasma lactate level is 0.3–1.3 mmol/L. Lactate > 2 mmol/L indicates hyperlactatemia. Lactic acidosis (LA) is defined as pH < 7.35 and lactate > 5 mmol/L. LA is the most common cause of metabolic acidosis in hospitalized patients. There are two subtypes of lactic acidosis. LA type A is usually due to tissue hypoxia, while type B is due to non-hypoxic causes related to lactate production and elimination. An increased or normal anionic gap or hypoalbuminemia may accompany LA. Severe acidemia has significant complications affecting all organs and systems. LA may impair myocardial contractility, reduce CO, sensitize the myocardium to arrhythmias, and render the CVS resistant to the action of catecholamines. Despite full-scale supportive treatment, the mortality rate due to LA is between 60% and 90%. In major surgeries, blood lactate levels with other hemodynamic parameters should be closely monitored to receive information about tissue oxygenation and perfusion. Monitoring blood lactate concentration should be considered for prognosis and as an indicator of how well supportive therapies treat tissue perfusion.[ ] LA treatment can be optimized by correcting the underlying cause, optimizing adequate tissue DO 2 , fluid resuscitation, restoring CO, and stabilizing hemodynamics. In the case of persistent oligoanuria due to AKI, emergency renal replacement therapy (RRT) may be necessary.[ ] Conclusion In the perioperative period, comprehensive preoperative assessment and correct preparation by the anesthesia team (anesthesiologist and nurses) and surgery with a multidisciplinary approach can determine the risk level, ensure patient safety, and optimize and significantly reduce mortality, morbidity, and the risk and severity of postoperative complications. The anesthesia team’s knowledge, attitude, experience, and multimodal approaches are critical in perioperative care. Effective communication and coordination between anesthesiologists, nurses, surgical teams, and other healthcare professionals are essential to provide comprehensive, high-quality, and effective patient care. In perioperative management, the five P (predictive, proactive, preventive, preventive, provisional) approach can be adapted to clinical practice [ ]. Early, adequate, individualized interventions to stabilize and improve homeostasis should be considered on a patient-by-patient basis. Adopting evidence-based guidelines, protocols, and algorithms in perioperative care and their best possible implementation will enable us to look to the future with more hope in improving the quality of anesthesia care, patient safety, and achieving better outcomes. Introduction The aorta is the main artery in the human body, responsible for carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle of the heart and out to the smaller arteries in the systemic circulation. Thus, diseases of the aorta affect the entire systemic circulation. Measurement of aortic diameters is one of the most widely used diagnostics of the aorta [ ]. As a biomarker, it is used to estimate the risk of rupture, dissection, and death [ , ] and is the main risk factor for aortic events [ ]. Additional studies have suggested that an enlarged diameter can be a biomarker of other adverse cardiovascular outcomes [ ]. Aortic dilation, including aortic aneurysms, has been associated with, for example, cardiovascular disease [ , ]. Computed Tomography (CT) is the current standard medical imaging modality for the diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy planning of aortic diseases [ ]. While Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (CMR) can assess the aorta’s shape, size, and tissue without the use of ionizing radiation, CT is used more often because it is more widely available and quicker to perform [ ]. Diameter measurements are usually performed manually on 2D CT scans using the inner-to-inner edge method at end-diastole [ ]. These intraluminal diameters should be measured at prespecified anatomical landmarks as the maximum distance perpendicular to the centerline. The aorta is typically divided into anatomical segments to define regional measurements, and AortaExplorer follows the definition of ESC [ ] as seen in Fig. . Other, more advanced, image-based biomarkers of aortic diseases include, among others, tortuosity. Tortuosity describes the amount of curvature of the blood vessel and is calculated as the ratio between the actual length of the vessel and the geometric length calculated as the Euclidean distance between the end points of the vessel [ ]. The tortuosity of the descending aorta has been shown to increase with age [ , ], due to structural changes in the elastin content of vessel walls, changes in the aortic length [ ], and decreased length of the vertebral column [ ]. A study in patients with Marfan syndrome found that aortic tortuosity independently predicted aortic dissections [ ], and higher tortuosity in the main arteries of the neck has been associated with earlier cardiac surgery, arterial dissection, and death in young adults with connective tissue disorders [ ]. However, tortuosity is still a fairly new biomarker and an area of research [ ]. In this paper, we present AortaExplorer : a fully automatic AI-based framework for the analysis of aortic anatomy from Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) scans. The purpose of AortaExplorer is to provide standard diagnostics such as aortic diameters in 3D, but also to serve as a research tool that allows exploratory analysis of additional cardiovascular risk predictors such as tortuosity. The framework is built using state-of-the-art building blocks such as TotalSegmentator[ ] for basic aorta segmentation and centerline extraction using the Vascular Modeling Toolkit (VMTK), combined with advanced refinement and fine-tuning for this specific application. The main contributions of our work are: Publication of an open-source research tool for fully automatic analysis from CTA scan to extracted aortic biomarkers Precise segmentation of the true aortic lumen Automatic identification of anatomical landmarks for separation into aortic segments Automatic computation of regional cross sectional areas and diameters in 3D Automatic extraction of aortic tortuosity Extensive validation based on manual annotations of aortic diameters in more than 10,000 CTA scans of the Danish general population Validation on several open aorta datasets including various aortic diseases Advanced visualization of aortic analysis for exploratory and research use AortaExplorer takes raw contrast-enhanced CTA scans as input and produces a comprehensive visualization of the aorta and its computed statistics. An overview of the pipeline is shown in Fig. . AortaExplorer is available for research use at https://github.com/RasmusRPaulsen/AortaExplorer/ . [ ] measured the aortic diameter from the outer wall to the outer wall using a deep learning-based method to segment the aorta. López-Linares et al. [ ] presented a framework for the detection of aortic lumen and infra-renal abdominal aortic aneurysms on CTA scans. The use of post-processing technology in CTA for diagnosing and classifying abdominal aortic aneurysms was also investigated by Yuan et al. [ ]. In the AortaSeg24 challenge [ ], participants were asked to develop algorithms for automatic segmentation of the aorta in 23 different segments and branches. The challenge was based on a dataset of 100 CTA scans with expert segmentation annotations. [ ] present an analysis of the tortuosity of the supra-aortic region using deep learning for aorta segmentation and a graph neural network for vessel labeling. Moking et al. [ ] perform semi-automatic computation of the tortuosity of the common carotid artery and the extracranial internal carotid artery. Many of the studies presented in this section relies on some kind of deep learning based methods to segment the aorta. The state-of-the-art for segmentation of most major anatomical structures in CT scans was transformed in 2023 with the publication of TotalSegmentator [ ]. TotalSegmentator is a robust deep learning-based tool trained on a large set of both CT scans with and without contrast to segment 117 main anatomical structures. TotalSegmentator makes the act of creating baseline segmentations for the aorta and other larger anatomical structures a trivial task, thus widening the landscape of potential research areas within the field of aortic analysis. In this work, we build on top of the best pre-trained models from TotalSegmentator and extend the usability to the more specialized domain of fine-grained aortic analysis. Aortic pathologies Aortic dilation, defined as an aortic diameter exceeding two standard deviations above the expected mean diameter, is the second most common aortic pathology [ ]. A localized dilation exceeding 150% of the predicted diameter constitutes an aortic aneurysm, which typically appears as a contrast-filled segment on CT images. In some cases, a minor leak in the aortic wall leads to an aneurysmic sac, where blood accumulates and coagulates; this structure is visible on CT but does not contain contrast-enhanced blood. An aortic dissection occurs when the intimal layer is breached, allowing blood to separate the layers of the wall. Most aneurysms are clinically silent–particularly abdominal aneurysms, where two-thirds of cases are asymptomatic [ ]. The primary symptomatic event is rupture, which is often fatal even with immediate intervention. Early management through medication or lifestyle modification is, therefore, critical to prevent rupture [ , , ]. Figure provides an overview of these aortic pathologies, while Fig. illustrates representative cases from the dataset. Although AortaExplorer is not intended for diagnostic use, severe cases appear in the external evaluation datasets. Data The Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS) is an ongoing prospective cohort study in Denmark. Since 2010, participants of at least 40 years of age with normal kidney function have been offered the opportunity to undergo a cardiac CTA research examination at Copenhagen University Hospital in Denmark. The scan protocol was extended with an abdominal CTA scan in 2014. Finally, a novel scan protocol was used to acquire the full aorta. The study protocol was approved by both a regional ethics committee (H-KF-01-144/01) and a local institutional review board. Participant consent is obtained for all cases analyzed. CTA image acquisition was performed using a 320-slice multi-detector computed tomography scanner. Abdominal and full aorta CTA was reconstructed with 0.5 mm slice thickness and increments of 0.30 mm, while cardiac CTA was reconstructed with 0.5 mm slice thickness and increments of 0.25 mm. Cardiac CTA was scanned using ECG gating in the 75% phase of the R-R interval. A complete description of the scan protocol is found in [ ]. To evaluate the performance of AortaExplorer, examinations using three different scan protocols are used: Cardiac CTA: with manual measurements of aortic diameters. External datasets for validation AortaExplorer robustness is evaluated by processing a set of open-source datasets of the aorta: The AortaSeg24 dataset [ ] contains 100 CTA images with associated ground truth segmentations of the aorta and its segments. Visual inspection of the images shows that most patients have a type B aortic dissection, which is a tear in the inner layer of the aorta that starts in the descending aorta (see Fig. ). Methods Each step seen in the analysis pipeline in Fig. is explained below. Basic segmentation and refinement The baseline segmentation of the aorta is computed using TotalSegmentator v.1.5 (TS) [ ] pre-trained total model. We also use the left ventricular (LV) and right ventricular (RV) blood pools computed using the heartchambers_highres pre-trained model. The TS segmentation of the aorta includes the full anatomical structure of the aorta, including the aortic wall, potential aneurysmal sacs, calcifications, and dilations. To allow for comparison with the measurement protocol in clinical practice, an accurate segmentation of the pure lumen (contrast-enhanced blood) is needed. Therefore, the TS segmentations need to be sub-segmented into a pure lumen and a calcification segmentation. An AortaExplorer result can be seen in Fig. . The original TS segmentation includes blood (lumen), calcifications, and the aortic wall. A skeleton is generated from the TS segmentation using morphological skeletonization [ ] and dilated by 1 mm to represent pure lumen voxels. Their Hounsfield unit (HU) values are sampled to compute the mean ( ) and standard deviation ( ). Following [ ], the lumen is estimated as connected voxels within the HU range , excluding low HU values from the aortic wall and high HU values likely corresponding to calcifications. Morphological opening and closing are applied as post-processing to remove holes and outliers. An ablation study is carried out in section to assess the effect of changing the thresholding parameters. Centerline extraction The aorta centerline is computed using the vascular modeling toolkit (VMTK) [ ] which, based on a surface representation of the aorta and a start and an end point, provides a centerline that follows the centers of the maximally inscribed spheres in the aorta. The surface of the aorta is computed using a discrete marching cubes algorithm on the segmentation of the lumen of the aorta [ ]. For full-aorta and abdominal-aorta scans, the start point is the iliac bifurcation identified from the TS aorta and iliac segmentations. The abdominal aorta end point is where the aorta leaves the upper scan range, while the full-aorta end point is on the LV at the distal aortic connection. For cardiac scans, the descending aorta uses the scan entry and exit points, whereas the ascending aorta starts where it leaves the scan and ends on the LV at the distal aortic connection. The centerline found by VMTK is approximated by a smoothing spline [ ] to remove minor fluctuations and to robustly compute the local tangent. From the tangent

The centerline found by VMTK is approximated by a smoothing spline [ ] to remove minor fluctuations and to robustly compute the local tangent. From the tangent and a defined up-vector, the normal and binormal can also be computed. The tangent, normal, and binormal form a local coordinate frame. This is also called a Frenet-Serret frame. A regularization step avoids sharp changes in the frames along the curve as described in [ ]. An inflection point of a curve is where a change in the direction of curvature occurs. This will induce a flipping of the curve normal. Following [ ], the dot product between the normal of the previous position on the curve and the normal at the current position is computed and if negative, the normal in the current position is flipped. This ensures a stable propagation of frames along the curve without flipping normals. See Fig. (left) for an example of a spline approximation of a centerline (gray points), with the local frames shown. The local frames are used in the following curved planar reformatting. Curved planar reformatting Curved Planar Reformatting (CPR) exploits the tubular structure of the aorta, resampling it in order to produce a straightened vessel [ ]. CPR maps from the original scanning space to a new space, where the vessel is straight. The main principle of this mapping is illustrated in Fig. (right). Each point on the curved centerline defines the origin in a local coordinate system defined by the regularized Frenet-Serret frames computed on the centerline, such that the xy-axes span a plane orthogonal to the curve. A user defined sampling distance can be used to sample slices along the curve and stacking them into the final straight volume. An example of a straightened volume can be seen in Fig. . The lumen segmentation is also straightened and used to calculate cross-sectional areas and diameters. Identification of aortic landmarks We follow the 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases [ ] to divide the aorta into anatomical segments and the identification of anatomical landmarks, as seen in Figs. and . Our landmark detection method works by first locating anatomical landmarks based on the segmentations and then projecting these on the centerline. This divides the centerline into the corresponding anatomical segments. For a scan that contains the entire aorta, five points on the centerline are chosen as landmarks, dividing the aorta into anatomical segments; ascending, arch, descending, suprarenal and infrarenal, as shown in Fig. . The number of available landmarks depends on the scan type, as the field-of-view (FOV) varies between scans. The identification of landmarks begins at the ventricular–aortic junction, marked pink in Fig. (right), and proceeds along the centerline to the bifurcation, shown in dark red. The ventricular–aortic landmark represents the boundary between the left ventricle (LV) and the aorta. To compute its position, the LV segmentation from TS and the refined aortic segmentation are dilated, the center of mass of their overlap is calculated, and the nearest centerline point is assigned as the landmark. The landmarks on the aortic arch include the proximal aortic arch landmark at the origin of TS segmentation of the brachiocephalic trunk, and the distal aortic arch landmark that is approximately 2 cm distal to the TS segmentation of the left subclavian artery. The landmarks of the three arteries that originate in the aortic arch are determined in a similar fashion, using TS segmentations for the three arteries, applying dilation with a structuring element with a radius of 5 mm in both the artery segmentation and the refined segmentation of the aorta, and calculating the center of mass of the overlap. From these, the nearest corresponding points on the centerline are computed and the final aortic landmarks are calculated as shown in Fig. . The descending aorta extends from the distal arch landmark to the diaphragm. The approximate location of the diaphragm is estimated using the TS segmentations of the right ventricle (RV), located above, and the liver, located below, as shown in Fig. (left). Starting from the lowest RV point, the shortest RV–liver distance is iteratively computed, resulting in two points. Their midpoint defines the diaphragm, and the nearest centerline point becomes the diaphragm landmark (Fig. (right)). However, since this intersection is often poorly visualized due to limited contrast, the landmark is instead computed from kidney TS segmentations: the line connecting both kidney centers of mass is drawn, and the closest centerline point is selected as the renal landmark (Fig. (right)). In addition to these five segmental landmarks, three landmarks characterize the aortic root, as seen in Fig. . The sinus of Valsalva is located within 20 mm distal to the ventricular–aortic landmark; the point with the largest cross-sectional area within this segment is chosen. The sinotubular junction is identified as the smallest cross-sectional area between 5 and 25 mm beyond the sinus landmark. Finally, the aortic annulus is defined as the minimum cross-sectional area within 10 mm proximal to the ventricular–aortic landmark along the combined LV–aorta centerline. Extraction of aortic biomarkers AortaExplorer automatically extracts the following image-based aortic biomarkers: diameter measurements and cross-sectional areas at defined landmarks and aortic tortuosity. The cross-sectional area can be extracted from the straightened segmentation of the aortic lumen. Diameter measurements are performed where the cross-sectional area is the largest (smallest for the sinotubular junction and annulus) for each of the anatomical segments shown in Fig. (left), as well as the landmarks for the sinus of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, and annulus. The maximal diameter is defined as the maximally long line that goes through the center of mass of the cross section and hits the boundaries of the cross section. Blood vessels have characteristic curved shapes, and tortuosity of vessels is most commonly defined as the ratio between the actual length of a vessel and the geometric length calculated as the Euclidean distance between the end points of the vessel [ ]. AortaExplorer computes two tortuosity measurements for the aorta: descending aortic tortuosity and full aortic tortuosity. The descending aortic tortuosity is calculated as the ratio between the geometric distance between the distal aortic arch and the diaphragm landmark and the actual distance following the center line between the two points. Similarly, the full aortic tortuosity is computed using the geometric and center line distances between the iliac bifurcation and the ventricularaortic landmark. Visualization AortaExplorer is intended as a research tool for the exploratory analysis of the aorta. It is therefore crucial to provide high-quality visualizations of the results for human visual validation and as a learning tool. For each case, a visualization as seen in Fig. is rendered as a PNG file. The visualization includes from left to right: metadata and extracted biomarkers; surface rendering of the aorta segmentation in two different views with indication of separation into aortic segments and excluded calcifications; CPR representation of the aorta in two planes with segmentation outline and diameter measurement locations drawn on top of the CTA scans; cross sectional CTA slices of the aorta at diameter measurement locations; volume rendering of the body from the CTA scan. At the bottom of the visualization is a plot of the cross-sectional area of the aorta along the centerline with markings where diameters are measured. All visualizations are performed using a combination of SimpleITK [ ] and the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) [ ]. Surface rendering is done by first transforming segmentations into triangulated surfaces using marching cubes [ ]. The volume rendered body is done by a GPU accelerated VTK renderer using a custom look-up table for tissue colors and opacities. Detection of failure cases AortaExplorer implements multiple safeguards to handle incomplete scans and acquisition errors. The first step determines the scan’s field-of-view (Fig. ) by assessing whether the aorta appears as a single structure or two separate segments, as in cardiac scans. A landmark-based heuristic then classifies the scan as complete, abdominal, or a two-part cardiac scan. Additional checks identify partial coverage, such as missing descending aorta. Subsequent analysis is restricted to well-defined cases. After lumen segmentation, the surface-to-volume ratio is computed. High ratios indicate a rough or porous lumen surface, typically reflecting non-contrast imaging or acquisition artifacts. This metric successfully flagged mislabeled non-contrast scans during development. For each cross-sectional slice, the aspect ratio of the best-fitting ellipse is also evaluated; if it exceeds a predefined threshold, the diameter estimate is discarded, and a warning is raised. Statistical analysis Aortic diameter measurements were evaluated against manual annotations using multiple metrics: mean absolute error (MAE), to quantify average deviation; mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), to show the estimation error compared to true aorta diameters; bias, also called mean error, to assess over- or underestimation. Furthermore, estimated diameters and manual measurements were evaluated as an inter-observer study by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient between the two variables and the coefficient of variation. The coefficient of variation is estimated as the relative bias by computing the mean of the difference between automated and manual estimates over the average of the two estimates as in [ ]. Bland-Altman analysis was performed to evaluate inter-observer (AI versus manual) agreement. All statistical tests for tortuosity were performed using the Python library scipy . Normality was tested using the Shapiro Wilk test. Comparison of mean values in two groups was performed using the t -test for normally distributed data and using the Mann-Whitney U-test for non-normally distributed data. Linear regression analysis was used to assess the effect of age on tortuosity. A significance level of was used for all analyzes. Results The aim of AortaExplorer is to enable AI-driven image reading for aortic analysis. The results produced by the pipeline contain a mixture of visualizations along with the computed statistics of the aorta, including the measurement of diameters at several landmarks and the tortuosity index. An example of an AortaExplorer analysis can be seen in Fig. . Experiments were conducted on a desktop system with 128 GB RAM, an AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D CPU, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU (12 GB VRAM). Total analysis time, including TotalSegmentator, was approximately five minutes per scan. Peak GPU memory usage was 8 GB during segmentation, and peak CPU memory usage was about 10 GB per process. The implementation is not optimized for speed, and runtime could thus be reduced further. AortaExplorer supports NIFTI, NRRD, and DICOM formats, enables batch processing of large datasets, and uses a multi-processing framework that leverages all available CPU cores. The software has been tested in a Danish hospital and runs on consumer-grade hardware. Additional details and examples are available on GitHub . to focus on the contrast-enhanced lumen. Discussion In this study, we introduce AortaExplorer, a comprehensive tool designed for end-to-end analysis of the aorta from CTA scans. AortaExplorer facilitates the extraction of image-based biomarkers and visualization of analytical output by integrating state-of-the-art methods, such as TotalSegmentator, as the basis for our aorta analysis. Although TotalSegmentator provides excellent initial segmentations, our evaluations revealed that refinement of these segmentations is crucial. Refinement helps with an accurate estimate of the aortic diameters by removing calcifications and the aortic wall from the segmentations. Furthermore, incorporating information about the surrounding organs allows us to accurately estimate the annulus landmark, which is not captured in the raw TS segmentation. The refinement results in large improvements in the mean absolute error between manual and AortaExplorer measurements: the smallest improvement is observed for the infrarenal diameter with a decrease of 43%, while the largest improvement is observed for the sinus of Valsalva diameter with a 70% reduction in mean absolute error. AortaExplorer has undergone extensive validation using more than 10,000 CTA scans from the CGPS cohort. AortaExplorer extracts five main landmarks, dividing the aorta into its anatomical segments, and three additional landmarks at the aortic root. Six of these segments and landmarks correspond to manual measurements: annulus, sinus of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending, descending, and infrarenal diameters. The tool demonstrated high and robust performance in estimating all six diameters in the large-scale dataset. AortaExplorer was evaluated on three publicly available aortic CTA datasets and demonstrated performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in terms of Dice similarity scores. In addition to segmentation accuracy, AortaExplorer provides comprehensive visualization tools and quantitative measurements, enabling detailed anatomical assessment beyond what is typically offered by existing approaches. In certain scenarios, validating automated measurements against manual readings is impractical due to time constraints or the complexity of specific measurements. In such cases, visualization becomes critical for quality assurance. Based on the visualization from AortaExplorer, as illustrated in Fig. , an experienced medical reader can quickly assess whether segmentation and landmark estimation were successful and if the extracted measurements can be trusted. Since a complete manual aortic analysis takes around 15 minutes, this method can drastically reduce the reading time, while maintaining high quality through human expert control. This would also be necessary to identify outliers or extreme estimation errors. Although existing studies provide reference values for aortic tortuosity based on analyzes of limited patient groups (200 and 182 patients, respectively [ , ]), and manual assessment for normal aortic diameter ranges (902 CT scans [ ]), our current study advances this work by evaluating both full aortic and descending aortic tortuosity on 1,144 scans along with diameter measurements on 10,000 scans. This demonstrates the ability of tools like AortaExplorer to accelerate manual assessment tasks and allow the extraction of advanced geometric biomarkers in large cohort studies. The 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases [ ] highlight the need for novel individualized risk stratification parameters beyond traditional markers for aortic aneurysms. AortaExplorer addresses this gap by enabling researchers to explore novel image-based biomarkers through possible custom-build functionalities built on top of our validated aorta segmentation and landmark detection. As an open-source tool, AortaExplorer has potential for extensive clinical research applications. It facilitates large-scale analysis of established image-based aortic biomarkers, enabling clinical researchers to establish reference values for these biomarkers on a large cohort scale. Furthermore, the adaptability of the tool enables exploratory research for the discovery of new image-based biomarkers. Calcifications, identifiable due to their high X-ray attenuation and HU values, pose a challenge in contrast-enhanced scans where patient-specific HU values in contrast-enhanced blood complicate identification. An extensive robustness analysis was performed on the HU threshold parameters, and it was found that the default parameters provide a robust estimate of the ratio of calcification. Future research will focus on the possibility of deriving a ground truth calcification measure that can be used to further develop and validate calcification detection from AortaExplorer. Conclusion In conclusion, this study presents AortaExplorer as a comprehensive tool for automated aortic analysis from CTA scans. By incorporating advanced segmentation refinement techniques, AortaExplorer significantly improves the accuracy of aortic diameter estimations from the TotalSegmentator baseline segmentations. Validated through extensive evaluation on a large-scale population data set, as well as smaller open source data sets, the tool demonstrates robust performance and offers clinical researchers the ability to conduct detailed cohort studies and explore novel biomarkers with efficiency and precision. Furthermore, AortaExplorer is open-source, making it a great resource for research on established and exploratory aorta biomarkers.

Central Message Transatrial transcatheter mitral valve replacement in severe MAC is durable with high technical success and acceptable mortality, offering a viable option for high-risk patients unsuitable for MVR. Perspective Mitral valve replacement in patients with severe MAC remains a complex challenge because of high surgical risk and anatomical constraints. This study demonstrates that transatrial transcatheter mitral valve replacement is durable and offers high technical success with favorable procedural outcomes, reinforcing its role as a valuable option for select high-risk patients with limited alternatives. Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is a chronic, noninflammatory, degenerative process involving the fibrous support structure of the mitral valve. Its prevalence is variable and strongly age-dependent. In a study of all the echocardiograms performed at the Mayo Clinic in 2015, MAC was identified in 23% of patients. The incidence and severity of MAC increases with advancing age and is associated with traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as atherosclerosis and chronic kidney disease. Although MAC does not always result in clinically significant mitral valve dysfunction, progressive disease may involve the valvular apparatus, leading to mitral stenosis, regurgitation, or mixed disease. It has been found that significant mitral valve dysfunction is more than twice as prevalent in patients with MAC. Furthermore, MAC is independently associated with increased risk of mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and atrial fibrillation. , The greatest mortality is observed in patients with MAC who also have significant mitral valve disease. Although surgical and transcatheter treatment improves the outcomes of patients with severe mitral valve disease and MAC compared with the use of medical management, both are associated with significant technical challenges and imperfect outcomes. Surgery is associated with operative mortality, risk of mitral annular disruption, and circumflex artery injury, whereas transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is associated with death, paravalvular leak (PVL), device migration, and left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. In patients with severe MAC who are not candidates for conventional surgical mitral valve replacement (MVR) or for transcatheter transseptal TMVR, the open transatrial (TA) approach using a balloon-expandable aortic valve represents a promising solution. Previous reports of open TA-TMVR have had variable results. There is a need for more robust, single-institution data to assess the feasibility, safety, and mid- and long-term outcomes of this technique in the setting of severe MAC. We report one of the largest single-institutional experiences with TA-TMVR using a balloon-expandable aortic valve in the setting of severe MAC. Methods We reviewed 25 consecutive patients who underwent open TA-TMVR using a balloon-expandable valve for severe MAC from 2014 to 2024 at the Mayo Clinic. The Mayo Clinic institutional review board approved the study (#24-005982, August 7, 2024), and consent was obtained from all patients to participate in research, including consent for publication. Inclusion criteria included the presence of severe MAC with symptomatic mitral valve disease in patients at high or prohibitive technical risk for conventional MVR surgery. The decision against standard MVR was made by an experienced mitral surgeon on the basis of patient characteristics and the extensiveness of MAC. Patients were also considered for TA-TMVR if they required concomitant procedures. Those who did not require additional procedures were reviewed by interventional cardiologists and were considered unsuitable for TMVR because of anatomy, MAC distribution, or risk of LVOT obstruction. Clinical, echocardiographic, cardiac computed tomography (CT), and operative data were collected from the institution's electronic medical records. Vital status was determined from LexisNexis Accurint, which links information from multiple sources, including the Social Security Death Master File and state death records. The reported death date from any of these sources was used; otherwise, patients were considered alive and were censored 2 weeks before the date their vital status was queried. The primary end point was technical success, defined as successful implantation of the transcatheter valve without need for conversion to conventional surgery or intraoperative mortality. Secondary end points included mortality, presence of PVL, postoperative complications, and subsequent interventions. Surgical Technique The surgical technique for TA-TMVR with a balloon-expandable valve has been previously described. , , Surgical technique evolved over the study period, and refinements included scalloping of the anterior valve skirt to reduce the risk of LVOT obstruction, use of guiding sutures for precise atrial positioning, and the addition of a felt strip to reinforce atrial fixation. We perform the procedure via median sternotomy with the patient undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass. Left atrial access is achieved either through a left atriotomy or a transseptal approach, depending on the patient's anatomy and the need for concomitant procedures. The mitral valve is assessed, with particular attention to the extent, distribution, and severity of MAC. A CT scan taken preoperatively is reviewed in all cases to assess the predicted neo-LVOT area using virtual valve modeling. A neo-LVOT area <2.0 cm 2 is considered high risk. Additional high-risk features included basal septal hypertrophy, acute aortomitral angle,

Left atrial access is achieved either through a left atriotomy or a transseptal approach, depending on the patient's anatomy and the need for concomitant procedures. The mitral valve is assessed, with particular attention to the extent, distribution, and severity of MAC. A CT scan taken preoperatively is reviewed in all cases to assess the predicted neo-LVOT area using virtual valve modeling. A neo-LVOT area <2.0 cm 2 is considered high risk. Additional high-risk features included basal septal hypertrophy, acute aortomitral angle, and heavy anterior leaflet calcification impeding displacement. If high risk for LVOT obstruction, a transverse aortotomy is performed, and a transaortic septal myectomy is carried out in a standard fashion. In addition, the anterior mitral leaflet and its chordae is resected to further reduce the risk of LVOT obstruction, whereas the posterior leaflet is left intact. The size of the valve is determined by a CT scan taken preoperatively and direct measurement of the mitral annulus diameter. The appropriate-sized SAPIEN aortic valve (Edwards Lifesciences) is selected and prepared on the back table. A felt skirt, approximately 10 to 15 mm in height, depending on valve size, is sewn circumferentially around the inflow portion of the valve using a running 4-0 PROLENE suture (Ethicon) to enhance sealing against the calcified annulus. One third of the skirt is scalloped to avoid LVOT obstruction. The valve is partially crimped with the scalloped portion aligned toward the LVOT ( , A ). Three guiding sutures of 2-0 PROLENE are placed at the anterolateral, posteromedial, and midpoint of the posterior annulus, approximately 120° apart. The guiding sutures are passed through the midsection of the stent at the corresponding commissures of the valve skirt to aid in orientation during deployment and allow for a more atrial position. The valve is then lowered into position and secured with Rummel tourniquets. Care is taken to maintain coaxial alignment during valve descent to prevent tilting or asymmetric deployment, especially in heavily asymmetric MAC. A balloon is inserted into the SAPIEN valve and inflated to nominal volume to deploy the valve. Balloon inflation is performed slowly under direct visualization. For ease of deployment, we use the Certitude delivery system. After deployment, the 3 guiding sutures are tied. Circumferential 2-0 pledgeted ETHIBOND sutures are then placed through the atrial side of the stent, atrial tissue and an additional felt strip ( , B ). The left ventricle is filled with saline to assess leaflet mobility and detect PVL. Transesophageal echocardiography is performed to confirm valve positioning, assess transvalvular gradients, and verify the absence of PVL or LVOT obstruction. Results Study Population Among the 25 patients included in the study, 17 (68%) were female, the mean age was 75 years, and all patients had severe MAC ( ). The average MAC score among patients in whom it was calculated was 9.5. Patients were considered prohibitive risk for conventional MVR if annular calcification was extensive and circumferential, such that annular decalcification and reconstruction would carry unacceptable risk of atrioventricular-groove disruption or injury to adjacent structures. Other prohibitive features included deep extension into the subannular left ventricular myocardium, bulky leaflet calcification that limited adequate annular suture placement, and anticipated inability to implant an adequately sized prosthesis without patient-prosthesis mismatch. In all cases, the final decision was made by an experienced mitral surgeon on the basis of annular anatomy and overall operative risk. The average body mass index was 32.3 kg/m 2 . The majority of patients (76%) were New York Heart Association functional class III or IV preoperatively. Twelve patients (48%) had undergone previous cardiac surgery, including coronary artery bypass grafting (n = 4, 16%), aortic valve replacement (AVR; n = 4, 16%), mitral valve repair (n = 4, 16%), and tricuspid valve repair (n = 1, 4%). Mitral stenosis was severe in 23 patients (92%), and 13 patients (52%) had moderate or severe mitral regurgitation. Seven patients (28%) had moderate or severe tricuspid valve regurgitation. The mean pulmonary artery systolic pressure was 51.5 mm Hg (range, 30-87 mm Hg). Baseline echocardiographic data are reported in . The most common was AVR in 11 patients (44%, all with bioprosthesis). Concomitant coronary artery bypass grafting was performed in 3 patients (12%). One patient (4%) underwent tricuspid valve replacement, another patient (4%) underwent tricuspid valve repair, and 4 patients (16%) had atrial septal defects closed. Septal myectomy was performed in 6 patients (24%) to mitigate the risk of LVOT obstruction. Complete anterior leaflet resection was performed in 23 patients (92%), and 1 patient (4%) underwent partial leaflet resection. Most valves were modified by adding a felt skirt sewn circumferentially around the inflow portion of the prosthesis to enhance sealing. After technique refinement, the anterior one third of the skirt was scalloped to reduce bulk in the LVOT and oriented toward the anterior mitral annulus to mitigate the risk of obstruction. A SAPIEN 3 transcatheter heart valve (Edwards Lifesciences) was implanted in 24 patients (96%), and 1 patient received a SAPIEN XT valve (4%). Valve sizes were 26 mm in 1 patient (4%) and 29 mm in 24 patients (96%). Valve sizing was determined on the basis of preoperative CT annular measurements, intraoperative direct sizing, and surgeon judgment. Our strategy was to implant the largest feasible valve to minimize risk of PVL while avoiding oversizing and potential annular disruption. Intraoperative characteristics are reported in . Operative Outcomes There were no intraoperative mortalities or atrioventricular-groove disruption. One patient experienced a perforation of the lateral wall of the left ventricle from the delivery system that was successfully repaired primarily and reinforced with felt. Operative mortality was 12%. All 3 patients died from multiorgan system failure associated with ischemic bowel. The average length of hospital stay was 14 days. Delayed sternal closure was used in 4 patients because of hemodynamic instability or coagulopathy. Two patients (8%) required reoperation for bleeding. One area of bleeding was identified at the pericardium, and another was at the aortotomy site. No patients experienced postoperative stroke. Other complications included renal failure requiring dialysis in 6 (25%). Prolonged ventilation (>48 hours) was required in 6 patients (24%), and 7 patients (33%) required permanent pacemaker implantation during the index hospitalization. Postoperative echocardiography revealed a mean left ventricular ejection fraction of 64% and a mean mitral valve gradient of 5 mm Hg. PVL was identified in 6 patients (24%), including 2 with mild and 4 with moderate regurgitation. Three of these patients underwent successful transcatheter PVL closure at 3 weeks, 1 month, and 4 months postoperatively. Two patients required PVL closure because of hemolysis. The other was experiencing worsening dyspnea. One of the patients who underwent PVL closure had ongoing hemolysis and underwent percutaneous transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve with a 26-mm SAPIEN 3 Ultra valve. No patients developed hemodynamically significant LVOT obstruction, valve migration, or embolization. No additional deaths occurred within 30 days after surgery. At 1 year, 8 patients had died, corresponding to a 68% survival rate. This included 3 operative deaths as previously described and 5 additional deaths during follow-up. Of these 5 patients, 2 died from noncardiac death (renal failure and worsening dementia) and 1 died from a cardiac arrest during an endoscopy. The cause of death in the remaining 2 patients was unknown. Survival at 3 and 5 years was 59.5% and 50.6%, respectively ( ). There were no known deaths attributable to structural valve dysfunction, valve thrombosis, endocarditis or other valve-related complications during follow-up. Postoperative outcomes are reported in . Discussion Patients with severe MAC face elevated surgical morbidity and mortality as a result of their underlying disease and associated comorbidities. Although intervention in this population is associated with improved survival compared with medical management, the procedural risks remain substantial, particularly with standard surgical MVR. As a result, operation is often deferred until patients become significantly symptomatic and debilitated. Consequently, the optimal treatment strategy for these high-risk patients remains a clinical challenge for cardiologists and cardiac surgeons. The least-invasive treatment approach is transseptal TMVR via transfemoral access. Despite its theoretical advantages, the transseptal approach is limited by several procedural challenges, including risk of valve malposition, migration, PVL, and LVOT obstruction. Clinical outcomes are variable, with many studies reporting low technical success and high mortality rates. Consequently, the optimal treatment strategy for these high-risk patients remains a clinical challenge for cardiologists and cardiac surgeons. The least-invasive treatment approach is transseptal TMVR via transfemoral access. Despite its theoretical advantages, the transseptal approach is limited by several procedural challenges, including risk of valve malposition, migration, PVL, and LVOT obstruction. Clinical outcomes are variable, with many studies reporting low technical success and high mortality rates. The Valve-in-MAC Global Registry, 2012-2015, a multicenter study analyzing 116 patients undergoing TMVR via transseptal, transapical, or TA access, found an overall technical success in 76.7% with 14.7% requiring a second valve. LVOT obstruction was seen in 11.2%. The 30-day mortality was 25% and the 1-year mortality was 53.7%. Among the different approaches, the TA group had a lower risk of mortality at 1 year compared with transseptal and transapical approaches. This is consistent with the early results of the study, where TA access was noted to have higher technical success and lower 30-day mortality. A study from the STS/American College of Cardiology Transcatheter Valve Therapy Registry identified 903 patients who underwent valve-in-valve, valve-in-ring, and valve-in-MAC. There were 100 patients who underwent TMVR for valve-in-MAC, of whom only 2% had TA access. LVOT obstruction occurred in 10% of patients, and 30-day mortality was 21.8%. Valve-in-MAC had the lowest procedural success rate and the greatest reintervention rate compared with valve-in-ring and valve-in-valve procedures. These studies, as well as the study by Yoon and colleagues, underscore the technical difficulty and elevated mortality risk associated with TMVR in MAC, particularly when performed via transseptal approaches. The authors of the Mitral Implantation of Transcatheter Valve (MITRAL) trial evaluated all 3 access routes in 31 patients with valve-in-MAC. Sixty-one patients (66%) were excluded because of high risk for LVOT obstruction or valve embolization. Patients were treated with pre-emptive alcohol ablation to help prevent LVOT obstruction, most frequently in patients who underwent a transseptal approach. Among those included, TA technical success was 73.3%, compared with 80% for transseptal access. Thirty-day mortality was 16.7% overall (TA 21.4%, transseptal 6.7%) and 1-year mortality was 34.5% (TA 38.5%, transseptal 26.7%). Several smaller studies have specifically investigated TA-TMVR. Operative mortality and major adverse cardiac events occurred in 10.4% and 22.5% of patients, respectively. Despite variability, these dedicated TA studies report consistently high technical success, consistent with our findings. Our study achieved 100% technical success with a 12% 30-day and 32% 1-year mortality. LVOT obstruction was not observed, and 3 patients required percutaneous PVL closure during follow-up. One of those patients required percutaneous valve-in-valve for ongoing hemolysis after PVL closure. Among patients who developed PVL requiring transseptal closure, only trivial PVL was detected intraoperatively on echocardiography, with the greatest degree of periprosthetic regurgitation being mild.
