Future RCTs are needed to evaluate the optimal timing and procedural strategy of prophylactic VT ablation. Furthermore, catheter ablation targeting triggers for PVT/VF can be effective in preventing PVT/VF recurrence. Clinical decision-making and planning cardiac ablation procedural approaches will benefit from the assessment of the competing risks of MMVT and PVT/VF. In this large, multicentre study, we, for the first time, developed and internally validated predictive models for the 3-year competing risk of MMVT and PVT/VF. We used state-of-the-art analytical approaches, including novel IPA assessment. The predictive accuracy of models was carried out on permuted set-aside validation samples. Both MMVT and PVT/VF models were determined to be useful according to IPA, demonstrating ROC(t)AUC of 0.7–0.9. The MMVT model demonstrated satisfactory calibration in high-risk patients with a 3-year probability of MMVT above 50%. The calibration of the PVT/VF model was satisfactory throughout the full range of probabilities. The successful development and validation of the MMVT and PVT/VF predictive models in this study open avenues for future RCTs of prophylactic MMVT ablation. In a similar to the PAUSE-SCD RCT patient population, our MMVT risk score identified 35% of patients with a 3-year probability of MMVT above 50%. Enrolment of patients with a 3-year probability of MMVT > 50% will be important for future RCT efficiency. Importantly, the clinical usefulness of our predictive models also should be tested in future RCTs. Strengths/limitations The strengths of the study include a large, multicentre study sample, including a diverse patient population. Notably, the study included patients with all Food and Drug Administration-approved types of implantable defibrillators (transvenous and subcutaneous ICD and CRT-D) manufactured by four major device makers (Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Abbott, and Biotronik). The diversity of patients, implanted devices, and device programming ensured the generalizability of the study findings. However, study limitations need to be considered. Due to the retrospective observational cohort study design, unmeasured confounding should always be considered. As we did not collect the data of induced MMVT CL, we were not able to replicate the PAUSE-SCD RCT device programming exactly, requiring the VT detection zone to be 10 bpm slower than induced MMVT. Dynamic changes in ECG and VCG metrics were not assessed and should be studied in future studies. Furthermore, the calibration of predictive models on a validation sample was suboptimal. Larger studies are needed to improve the models’ accuracy. Only 30% of the study population had a device implanted in the most recent era of HF GDMT. However, the incidence of PVT/VF has not changed over time, supporting the contemporary relevance of our study findings. Furthermore, adjustment for the therapeutic era had no effect on the study findings. Nevertheless, a fast-developing field of implantable devices and further improvement in HF therapies will likely require regular updates of predictive models in the future. Conclusion In this large, contemporary multicentre study of systolic HF patients with primary prevention ICD and modern programming, we developed and validated a 3-year competing risk of MMVT and PVT/VF models accounting for competing risk of death without VT/VF. The MMVT predictive model determined that 35% of patients had a >50% probability of developing sustained MMVT with appropriate ICD therapy within the first 3 years. The threshold of high-risk (>50%) MMVT had 75% sensitivity and 65% specificity. Furthermore, we identified cause-specific risk factors for MMVT and PVT/VF, facilitating personalization of future management. The clinical usefulness of the models should be further tested in prospective studies, including RCTs of prophylactic MMVT catheter ablation. Supplementary Material euae127_Supplementary_Data

1 Introduction Sodium-glucose co-transporter protein-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have been shown to reduce the incidence of hospitalization for exacerbations and cardiovascular event mortality in adult chronic cardiac failure (CHF) patients in numerous clinical studies and has been recommended as one of the four cornerstone pharmacological therapies for the treatment of CHF by several guidelines ( – ). Dapagliflozin, a classic representative of SGLT2i, has been widely used in the treatment of adult CHF, but few studies have addressed its efficacy and safety in pediatric CHF patients ( – ). CHF in children is often complicated by various types of cardiovascular diseases, including congenital heart disease, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, and arrhythmia, of which heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) represents an important clinical subtype in clinical practice ( – ). If the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin can be verified in pediatric HFrEF cases, it will undoubtedly bring new hope for the treatment of such pediatric cases. The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in children with HFrEF and to explore safe dosing of dapagliflozin in children with HFrEF. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Materials A retrospective cohort study was used. Clinical data were extracted from electronic medical records. A total of 32 children with HFrEF who attended the Department of Cardiology of Shanghai Children's Medical Center and Fujian Children's Hospital from June 2021 to June 2023 and met the eligibility criteria were included as the study group. The eligibility criteria were (1) aged from 6 months to 18 years; (2) having received angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI) or angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), beta-blocker, or aldosterone receptor antagonist for at least 2 weeks but less than 4 weeks, had a two-dimensional echocardiogram that indicates a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of less than 40%, and had a New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification between I and III; and (3) estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥ 60 mL/(min·1.73 m 2 ). The exclusion criteria were (1) clinical assessment of children in NYHA class IV status; (2) children with conditions requiring vasoactive drug therapy; (3) children with blood pressure lower than P5 in children of the same sex and age; (4) children with any type of diabetes mellitus; (5) comorbidity with uncontrolled urinary tract infections; (6) comorbidity with other medical conditions such as hepatic and renal function abnormalities that may affect drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion; or (7) discontinuation of dapagliflozin during follow-up due to severe complications resulting in incomplete follow-up. Dapagliflozin was prescribed as off-label therapy as part of routine clinical care, and written informed consent for off-label drug use was obtained from the legal guardians according to institutional clinical practice. 42 children treated during the same period who received standard heart failure therapy without dapagliflozin were included as the control group. 2.2 Methods 2.2.1 Collect and analyze the children's clinical data The children's age, weight, gender, height, body mass index, blood pressure, clinical symptoms, NYHA cardiac function class, LVEF, type B natriuretic peptide (BNP), blood glucose, liver and kidney function, blood electrolytes, glomerular filtration rate, and so on were collected and analyzed. The baseline indexes before treatment were reviewed after receiving dapagliflozin treatment for 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, and 1 month, and followed up to 24 (±2) weeks month by month. 2.2.2 Treatment regimen All patients received guideline-directed triple therapy, including an ACEI/ARNI, a beta-blocker, and an aldosterone receptor antagonist, and doses were up-titrated as tolerated according to clinical condition. Patients were assigned to the control group if their guardians refused dapagliflozin because of concerns regarding its off-label use and potential risks. In addition, children in the dapagliflozin group were treated with dapagliflozin according to a weight-stratified dosing regimen. For pediatric patients weighing <10 kg, dapagliflozin was administered at a dosage of 0.2 mg/kg/d. Patients with a body weight ranging from 10 kg to less than 20 kg (20 > weight ≥10 kg) received dapagliflozin at a dose of 2.5 mg/d. Those weighing between 20 kg and less than 30 kg (30 > weight ≥20 kg) were prescribed dapagliflozin at 5 mg/d. For patients weighing 30 kg or more, the initial dose of dapagliflozin was 5 mg/d, which was increased to 10 mg/d after one month. 2.2.3 Observation indexes The main observation indexes were the changes of NYHA cardiac function class, LVEF, and BNP when receiving dapagliflozin treatment for 24 (±2) weeks. The secondary observation indexes were the occurrence of hospitalization or death due to exacerbation of CHF within 24 (±2) weeks of dapagliflozin treatment. Adverse medicine events such as hypoglycemia or hypotension were also observed during treatment. 2.2.4 Statistical methods Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 27.0 (IBM Corp.). No other adverse reactions, including hypoglycemia or liver and kidney function impairment, were observed at the final follow-up. 4 Discussion SGLT2i, a class of oral hypoglycemic agents, has become a rapidly emerging therapeutic option in the field of type II diabetes since its introduction ( , ). Surprisingly, this class of drugs has demonstrated cardiovascular event benefit in several clinical studies of type II diabetes combined with CHF, making it useful in the field of CHF treatment as well. It has been suggested ( , ) that SGLT2i can increase energy expenditure and free fatty acid oxidation, which in turn increases the level of β -hydroxybutyrate, a source of energy for cardiomyocytes, and thus improve energy metabolism in cardiomyocytes and cardiac function. HFrEF is a common clinical cardiovascular condition, characterized by poor overall prognosis and limited treatment options. In recent years, a number of high-level clinical guidelines in Europe and the United States have fully affirmed the benefits of SGLT2i in HFrEF patients and recommended it as one of the four basic drugs for HFrEF treatment. In August 2023, dapagliflozin was approved for the treatment of HFrEF by the National Medical Products Administration in China. However, few of the above guidelines or clinical studies involve pediatric cases. In 2022, Newland et al. ( ) first reported the use of dapagliflozin in children with dilated cardiomyopathy or single ventricle combined with CHF cases. In that study, a total of 37 children with HFrEF received dapagliflozin at an initial dose of 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/d and a maximum dose of 10 mg/d. The results suggested that dapagliflozin could effectively improve LVEF, BNP, and other clinical indicators in children. In the study, six children developed urinary tract infection and four children developed acute renal impairment, but all of them improved after treatment, suggesting that dapagliflozin was relatively well tolerated by children with HFrEF. Cui Jingyi et al. ( ) reported the results of a study of dapagliflozin in children with hereditary nephropathy associated with proteinuria, which also suggested the safety of dapagliflozin in children with hereditary nephropathy in different dose ranges. With reference to the above results, dapagliflozin at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg/d up to 10 mg/d was administered to children with HFrEF in different weight ranges. However, in the study, all children received a triple combination of ACEI/ARNI, beta-blocker, and aldosterone receptor antagonist in addition to dapagliflozin. In addition, 11 children in the dapagliflozin group received digoxin and two children underwent cardiac resynchronization therapy, while 12 children in the control group received digoxin and one child underwent cardiac resynchronization therapy. The treatment modalities were not identical between the two groups except for dapagliflozin. Therefore, the improvement in LVEF and BNP could not be attributed to dapagliflozin alone but was more likely to be the result of a combination of drugs and therapeutic measures. It should also be noted that NYHA functional classification was developed for adults, so its applicability in infants and young children is limited, and results should be interpreted with caution. Future studies may consider using age-appropriate tools such as the modified Ross Classification for Heart Failure in Children to better evaluate functional improvement. Previous studies about the usage of dapagliflozin have mainly focused on reducing the risk of death and hospitalization due to worsening heart failure. In the present study, all 32 children treated with dapagliflozin were alive at the last follow-up and did not require hospitalization for worsening heart failure during the 24 (±2) weeks of follow-up, showing a significant advantage over the control group. The latest guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure in Europe suggest that dapagliflozin significantly reduces the risk of hospitalization but not cardiovascular death ( ).However, our study provided novel insights as a real-world, bicenter cohort in China, focusing specifically on the dosing strategy of dapagliflozin, and the results suggested that dapagliflozin may provide additional benefit in children with HFrEF. However, the small sample size of this study and the fact that the underlying diseases in all cases included only dilated cardiomyopathy and congenital heart disease, with no coronary heart disease or ischemic cardiomyopathy, may explain the discrepancy between the results of the study and the adult guidelines. Recent national and international studies have further suggested that the therapeutic effect of dapagliflozin in CHF is independent of LVEF. Patients with mildly reduced ejection fraction or preserved ejection fraction can also benefit, contributing to strengthened recommendations for dapagliflozin ( – ). Further follow-up studies are needed to determine whether the same effect is seen in pediatric cases. In summary, dapagliflozin was associated with improved LVEF, reduced BNP levels, and improved NYHA cardiac functional classification, with no hospitalization or death because of worsening heart failure in children with HFrEF observed during short-term follow-up. The weight-stratified dosing regimen also demonstrated acceptable short-term tolerability. However, the sample size of this study is small and the follow-up period is not long; therefore, we look forward to increasing the sample size to provide further high-grade clinical evidence for dapagliflozin in pediatric heart failure patients.

Introduction Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has increased in recent years with rates now exceeding those of surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). , Whilst the expanding indications for TAVI are supported by evidence, there are variations in the delivery of TAVI care across the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) member countries, with an overall procedural volume ranging from 0.6 to 200 per million people. National registries have played an important role in exploring the patterns of TAVI care and outcomes. However, heterogeneity in design and delivery of TAVI registries limits the robust investigation of the effectiveness and safety of novel TAVI devices and adjunctive medications across countries. There is a lack of standardized definitions for TAVI registry variables. Even though the Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC) provides endpoint definitions for heart valvular interventions including TAVI, the definitions of clinical outcomes vary between TAVI studies. , Besides, VARC harmonizes outcome definitions, but there remains a need to standardize the methods by which the processes of TAVI care delivery are captured. Such a harmonization across TAVI registries, randomised controlled trials (RCTs), and quality improvement initiatives, improves the efficiency of data collection and help generate new knowledge relevant to TAVI. The American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA) have developed data standards for a range of cardiovascular diseases, but no ACC/AHA data standards exist for TAVI. The European Unified Registries On Heart Care Evaluation and Randomised Trials (EuroHeart) is an ESC initiative that aims to improve the quality of cardiovascular care through the continuous capture of individual patient data by standardizing the definitions of variables and offering a common IT platform for data collection, analysis, and reporting. To date, EuroHeart has developed data standards for acute coronary syndrome and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), heart failure and atrial fibrillation. This document presents the EuroHeart data standards for TAVI, which have been developed in collaboration with the European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI), the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging (EACVI) and the Working Group on Cardiovascular Surgery of the ESC. Methods The Data Science Group of EuroHeart was established in August 2019. It comprises a project chair (C.G.), two medical experts (S.A. and G.B.), a biostatistician (J.W.) and a project manager. Working group and reference group The Working Group for the development of the 2022 EuroHeart data standards for TAVI included 29 members from 12 countries. The Group comprised members of the EuroHeart Data Science Group and nominees from the EAPCI, EACVI and the Working Group on Cardiovascular Surgery, as well as leaders of existing TAVI registries and a patient representative. Further 19 experts from 18 countries formed the Reference Group (Acknowledgment) and provided feedback on the selection and definitions of the included variables in the EuroHeart TAVI dataset. European Unified Registries On Heart Care Evaluation and Randomised Trials data standards methodology We followed the EuroHeart methodology for cardiovascular data standard development. In brief, this involved: (1) identification of the cardiovascular domain for the development of data standards; (2) conduction of a systematic review of the literature to synthesise a list of ‘candidate’ variables; (3) selection and prioritisation of variables by domain experts using a modified Delphi method; (4) Reference Group feedback, and (5) programming the final data variables into the EuroHeart IT platform. Variable level In EuroHeart, variables are classified as Level 1 variables if they are needed for the assessment of the quality of care (for example, information that would be required for the calculation of quality indicators), risk stratification, case-mix adjustment, or clinical outcomes. The Level 1 variables are defined in the EuroHeart data standard documents and are programmed into the EuroHeart IT platform. Level 2 variables collect information that may prove useful for quality assessment and observational, or randomised research, but which may not be universally available, routinely used, or a pre-requisite for the evaluation of quality. The Level 2 variables are defined in the EuroHeart data standard documents but are not implemented into the EuroHeart IT platform. For the countries which adopt the EuroHeart IT platform, a third level of variables can be programmed into the platform to address unique centre- or country-specific requirements. Thus, the Level 3 variables are not defined in the EuroHeart data standard documents. EuroHeart aims to align international data collection activities and therefore countries with existing registries may not choose to implement the EuroHeart IT platform, but harmonize their data standards with the EuroHeart variables. Scope The Working Group agreed that the EuroHeart-TAVI registry should capture pre-procedural care processes as well as procedural details, in-hospital events and follow up data. As far as possible, the data definitions were aligned with these collected in other EuroHeart registries including heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, PCI and atrial fibrillation , allowing re-utilization of existing information and avoiding duplication in different registries. Thereby, the TAVI registry may, especially in the EuroHeart IT-platform, be integrated with these databases to form a unified system for data collection and quality improvement ( Figure ). Systematic literature review The EuroHeart Data Science Group conducted a systematic review of the literature to identify a list of candidate variables for potential inclusion in the EuroHeart TAVI dataset. The search included two databases (Embase and MEDLINE via OVID®) and captured peer reviewed RCTs and prospective observational studies that provided definitions for at least one variable relevant to TAVI diagnosis, management, or outcomes published between 01 January 2011 and 23 July 2021 (Appendix). Two reviewers (SA and GB) assessed retrieved articles against a pre-specified eligibility criteria and extracted potential variables from included studies. Existing TAVI registries and Clinical Practice Guidelines were also reviewed for potential data variables relevant to TAVI. Selection of the final set of variables Using a modified Delphi method, the Working Group voted on the list of candidate variables that were identified from the literature review. In total, two voting rounds and nine virtual meetings were conducted between April 2021 and January 2022, with a large volume of e-mail correspondence between meetings. The EuroHeart criteria for data standard development (importance, evidence base, validity, reliability, feasibility and applicability) were used to guide the selection process. The Working Group members voted on each of the candidate variables with include as Level 1, include as Level 2 or exclude. Variables achieved ≥75% agreement were included whilst those did not were carried to a second voting round and discussed in the subsequent meetings. The final set of variables was presented to the Reference Group for feedback on their validity and feasibility. Implementation After arriving at the final set of variables, the Data Science Group collaborated with the Registry Technology groups of the EuroHeart project to programme the Level 1 variables into the EuroHeart IT platform. The variables were structured in a chronological order from the pre-procedural details to the outcomes of TAVI. The platform was designed to improve the data entry consistency and reduce the burden of data entry. Results The systematic review retrieved 3225 articles. Of these, 372 met the inclusion criteria and were used to extract candidate variables. Following the modified Delphi method, 93 Level 1 variables (Supplementary material online, ) and 113 Level 2 variables (Supplementary material online, ) were selected for 10 domains of TAVI care. The domains of care in the EuroHeart TAVI registry are: (1) Demographics, (2) Patient characteristics and comorbidities, (3) Health-related quality of life, (4) Prior interventions, (5) Presentation details, (6) Pre-procedural tests, (7) Procedural details, (8) Outcomes, (9) Discharge details and (10) Follow up. Demographics This domain is purposefully aligned with the EuroHeart registries for acute coronary syndrome-PCI, heart failure and atrial fibrillation. , This reduces the amount of data that is needed to be entered for patients who are enrolled in more than one EuroHeart registry. The domain captures patient-identifiable information to allow data linkages (Supplementary material online, ) and is therefore only stored at the local centre or at country-level in accordance with the each country's data-sharing regulations. De-identified, aggregated data may be shared with the EuroHeart Data Science Centre to create high-level reports following agreements from relevant parties (Supplementary material online, ). Patient characteristics and comorbidities This domain contains information about the patient's characteristics (e.g. height and weight) at the time of hospital admission for the TAVI procedure. Baseline comorbidities (e.g. heart failure) and prognostic variables (e.g. frailty) are also captured because of the role of such variables in risk adjustment models and risk stratification scores for TAVI outcomes. Although the definitions of the variables are the same as those in the other EuroHeart registries, the domain also records TAVI specific variables such as the assessment of aortic calcification ( ). , Health-related quality of life Patient health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is important prior to invasive procedures, but its systematic collection in routine clinical practice is difficult. Thus HRQoL has been included as Level 2 variable in the EuroHeart-TAVI data standards (Supplementary material online, ). definitions of the variables are the same as those in the other EuroHeart registries, the domain also records TAVI specific variables such as the assessment of aortic calcification ( ). , Health-related quality of life Patient health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is important prior to invasive procedures, but its systematic collection in routine clinical practice is difficult. Thus HRQoL has been included as Level 2 variable in the EuroHeart-TAVI data standards (Supplementary material online, ). Prior interventions This domain captures information about aortic valve or other cardiac interventions (e.g. PCI) prior to the TAVI procedure ( ). The collection of information about prior SAVR and TAVI procedures contributes to the understanding of the characteristics and outcomes following valve-in-valve procedures given that TAVI in failed surgical bioprosthetic valves is now an established treatment and TAVI-in-TAVI may become an important treatment in the future. Presentation details This domain includes information about a patient's clinical status at the time of admission to hospital. It includes the presenting symptoms, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class and some ECG parameters ( ). The EuroHeart TAVI data standards enables patient risk stratification from the submitted variables and allows the entry of the EuroSCORE II (Supplementary material online, ). Data about cardiogenic shock, the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) grade of angina and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score are included as Level 2 variables (Supplementary material online, ). Pre-procedural tests The ESC guidelines recommend an assessment of coronary artery disease prior to invasive valve intervention. This domain collects information about concomitant coronary artery disease prior to a TAVI procedure, as well as biochemical (e.g. haemoglobin, creatinine) and echocardiographic parameters (e.g. left ventricular ejection fraction, mean aortic valve gradient) prior to the procedure (Supplementary material online, ). Information concerning the extent of aortic, leaflet and left ventricular outflow tract calcification are captured in this domain in addition to concomitant valvular (e.g. mitral) disease (Supplementary material online, ). A selection of the Level 1 variables is shown in Figure . Procedural details The specifications of the TAVI procedure are captured in this domain including the date of the procedure, type of anaesthesia, access site and valve types used (Supplementary material online, ). This domain collects information such as the planned concomitant interventions (e.g. PCI) as well as the use of cerebral embolic protection and/or vascular closure devices (Supplementary material online, ). Procedural events are included in this domain as Level 1 variables (Supplementary material online, Table S1 ) with additional details (e.g. pacing, circulatory support) as Level 2 (Supplementary material online, ). In-hospital data This domain captures the findings from echocardiography undertaken after the TAVI procedure and before hospital discharge (Supplementary material online, ). In-hospital events that occur after the TAVI procedure are also recorded here. These events include cardiac interventions during the same admission, in-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, bleeding or death (Supplementary material online, ). The definitions of these events are aligned with the VARC-3 criteria. Discharge details This domain records information about antithrombotic therapy and some ECG findings at the time of discharge from hospital (Supplementary material online, ). Biomarkers (e.g. haemoglobin, creatinine) other medications and referral for cardiac rehabilitation are included as Level 2 variables (Supplementary material online, ). Follow up All of the variables in this domain are Level 2. This is because concerns were raised about the feasibility of efficiently collecting patient information beyond the hospital stay. The domain defines variables to be collected after hospital discharge and specifies the intervals for their collection (Structured Graphical Abstract). Discussion The EuroHeart data standards for TAVI processes of care and in-hospital outcomes comprise 93 mandatory (Level 1) and 113 optional (Level 2) variables across 10 TAVI domains. They set forth an internationally agreed and ESC endorsed standards for the conduct of observational studies and RCTs that are relevant to TAVI, provide a platform for monitoring the effectiveness and safety of new devices and treatment strategies, and align with published EuroHeart data standards for other cardiovascular diseases. , The standardisation of the definitions of TAVI-related data variables enables the conduction of international comparative analyses and facilitates the development of a comprehensive registry for various forms of valvular heart disease regardless of its treatment strategy. Despite previous efforts, there remains a need for a harmonised, internationally endorsed and feasible set of data standards for TAVI encompassing both processes of care and key outcomes. , For instance the ACC and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Transcatheter Valve Therapy (TVT) registry comprises 216 variables, 160 of which are mandatory. efforts, there remains a need for a harmonised, internationally endorsed and feasible set of data standards for TAVI encompassing both processes of care and key outcomes. , For instance the ACC and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Transcatheter Valve Therapy (TVT) registry comprises 216 variables, 160 of which are mandatory. To reduce the burden of data collection, a recent collaboration between various stakeholders in the US was established to develop a ‘Minimum Core Data Elements' for TAVI. However, this dataset defined 132 mandatory variables and maintained an additional 35 variables as mandatory in the ACC/STS TVT registry increasing the total number to 167. Moreover, the definitions of the variables in the updated ACC/STS TVT registry have not been fully aligned with these in other relevant registries. For example, the definition of cerebrovascular disease varies between the ACC PCI and TVT registries limiting the opportunity to combine data from different resources. In Europe, national registries had an important role in illustrating the patterns of TAVI care and understanding its outcomes. However, the heterogeneity in the data standards between these registries hampers the conduction of pragmatic registry-based RCTs (R-RCT) and the performance of post-marketing surveillance of new TAVI technologies across borders. Furthermore, the lack of harmonisation between national TAVI registries and existing databases for other cardiovascular diseases (e.g. PCI) results in redundancy and unnecessary duplication of healthcare data collection. EuroHeart provides an umbrella under which standardised data definitions are developed and harmonised across various cardiovascular disease domains. The data standards for TAVI presented in this document have been developed in collaboration with the EAPCI the EACVI and the ESC Working Group on Cardiovascular Surgery and with involvement of a patient representative. Furthermore, the definitions of the selected variables were aligned with the ESC guidelines for valvular heart disease and the VARC endpoints. , Consequently, these standards were endorsed by the ESC Association of Cardiovascular Nursing and Allied Professions (ACNAP) and the ESC Committee for Young Cardiovascular Professionals, highlighting their potential role in evaluating and addressing the variation in TAVI care and outcomes within and between countries. , Developing internationally recognised standards for data collection may not necessarily guarantee their uptake in practice. For instance, the VARC clinical endpoints which aimed to harmonize the methods by which TAVI outcomes are defined have not been adopted in over 40% of TAVI studies. , This may be explained by the need to integrate process variables with outcomes in a single system, which the VARC lacks. Additionally, the implementation of the developed variables into a web-based interface may facilitate the uptake of the data collection system. The EuroHeart-TAVI data standards comprise key processes and in-hospital outcomes as Level 1 variables which are embedded into an IT platform, with additional variables that capture follow up data as Level 2. We anticipate that the EuroHeart-TAVI registry will provide the means for a wider valvular heart disease registry that capture data relevant to various treatment strategies. We recognise that countries may be interested in adopting the EuroHeart definitions and not implementing the EuroHeart-IT platform. Those countries can, of course, use the data standards presented in this document and modify their existing registries accordingly. Whilst long-term follow up outcomes are developed as Level 2 variables in the EuroHeart-TAVI dataset, harmonized clinical outcomes will be an integral component of the EuroHeart Data Standards for Clinical Outcome module which is currently under development. Adjudication of the imaging parameters or outcomes can be implemented to serve a future R-RCT that is conducted using the EuroHeart-TAVI IT platform. We acknowledge that the EuroHeart standards are not mapped to an electronic health record coding system that facilitates their syntactic interpretation—presently, this is beyond the remit of EuroHeart. The EuroHeart methodology relies on expert opinion to select the final set of variables and therefore may have been influenced by the participant bias. However, inclusiveness of the Working and Reference Groups, and the use of a modified Delphi method enabled the standardization of the selection process. Conclusions The EuroHeart data standards for TAVI processes of care and in-hospital outcomes are an internationally agreed and ESC endorsed set of standards that may be used for the conduct of observational studies, RCTs and TAVI devices surveillance. In total, 93 mandatory Level 1 variables are programmed into the EuroHeart IT platform and provide the core TAVI dataset. Introduction Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a cardiopulmonary disorder characterized by a progressive elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). It is defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) exceeding 20 mmHg at rest, and, if untreated, it will ultimately lead to right heart failure and death. According to the classification of the World Health Organization (WHO) and the new guideline for diagnosis of PH, it is categorized into five groups: pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), PH associated with left heart disease (PH-LHD), PH associated with lung diseases and/or hypoxia, PH associated with pulmonary artery obstructions, and PH with unclear and/or multifactorial mechanisms [ ], ]. The pathological remodeling of pulmonary vasculature in PH often originates from endothelial cell (EC) injury. This initial damage leads to endothelial dysfunction and apoptosis, compromising the vascular barrier. The loss of endothelial integrity and regulatory functions further propagates signals that activate adjacent smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and disrupt the equilibrium between vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive substances. Consequently, sustained vasoconstriction and a pro-proliferative state are established [ ]. Inflammatory signals exacerbate the complexity of this pathological milieu, feeding a self-amplifying cycle that drives key structural changes, including SMC hypertrophy/hyperplasia and vascular wall fibrosis. Collectively, these alterations constitute the irreversible remodeling of pulmonary arteries, ultimately leading to elevated PVR and right heart failure. The disease etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, metabolism, inflammation and other factors, many of which represent potential therapeutic targets or biomarkers. Notably, some targets are relevant for pediatric PH. Furthermore, advances continue to be made in clinical diagnosis, risk-stratified treatment strategies, drug development, surgical and interventional techniques, as well as imaging assessment and emerging modalities. Given the substantial advances in both basic research and clinical management of PAH over recent 10 years, this review will delve into the pathological mechanisms and contemporary therapeutic approaches in this pulmonary vascular disorder. Advancing the understanding of PH pathogenesis Genetics and gene regulation Genetic predisposition In the past two decades, a few susceptibility genes have been identified in PH, including BMPR2 , EIF2AK4 , ACVRL1 , ENG , CAV1 , KCNK3 , TBX4 , SOX17 , SMAD9 , ATP13A3 , GDF2 , KDR , ABCC8 , AQP1 , BMP10 , SMAD4 and SMAD1 . The discovery of these genes has reshaped our understanding of the disease. The bone morphogenetic protein receptor Type 2 (BMPR2) signaling axis Dysfunction of the BMPR2 pathway remains the central genetic driver in adults ( ). Multiple mechanisms compromise this receptor. For instance, the transcription factor TWIST1 promotes remodeling by degrading GATA-6, thereby suppressing BMPR2 expression [ ]. Similarly, endothelial overproduction of activin A triggers the lysosomal degradation of BMPR2 [ ]. Regulators of receptor stability are key targets. SMURF1 is overactive in PH and degrades BMPR2 [ ], and specific inhibitors targeting the SMURF1 HECT domain can restore signaling [ ]. BMPR2 mutations disrupt cardiac differentiation via ID genes [ ], promote PASMC dedifferentiation and fibrosis [ ], and upregulate β-arrestin 2, which activates proliferative Akt/β-catenin signaling [ ]. Endothelial consequences include reduced FOXF1 expression, which impairs DNA repair [ ]. Other pathway components are also involved. SMAD4 deficiency disrupts cell adhesion [ ], while GDF2 mutations lead to BMP9 loss [ ]. Crucially, germline mutations in GDF2 cause idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH) by reducing circulating BMP9 levels and impairing endothelial BMP signaling, confirming that a deficiency in the ligand (BMP9) can cause the same disease phenotype as a deficiency in the receptor (BMPR2) [ ]. Disrupted BMP-9 signaling has been linked to impaired pulmonary vascular integrity in hepatopulmonary syndromes [ ]. Clinically, dilated episcleral vessels are a marker for BMPR2 mutation carriers [ ]. Additionally, BMPER promotes remodeling by binding LRP1 to release YAP [ ]. SOX17 and angiogenic pathways Beyond the pediatric context, SOX17 governs critical homeostatic mechanisms ( ). Common risk variants in its enhancer reduce endothelial SOX17 expression [ ]. This deficiency triggers reactive HGF/c-Met signaling [ ] and upregulates HIF-2α/mitochondrial dysfunction [ ], while unleashing E2F1 to drive hyperproliferation [ ]. Angiogenic signaling is also critical. EIF2AK4 mutations drive pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD) [ ]. Similarly, mutations in KDR (VEGFR2) cause severe remodeling and fibrosis [ ], and Flk1 deficiency synergizes with hypoxia to trigger endothelial apoptosis [ ]. Large-scale Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have further mapped genetic loci associated with right ventricular (RV) function [ ]. Epigenetic regulation Developmental reversion and methylation Epigenetic regulation is central to PH pathogenesis, often involving the pathological reactivation of transcriptional programs that are normally active only during fetal lung development [ ]. This hypothesis is supported by evidence from neonatal PH models demonstrating a persistent “fetal-like” pattern of tropoelastin gene expression [ ]. DNA methylation modulates this landscape through a dynamic interplay of enzymes. DNMT3B has been identified as a protective mediator [ ]. Epigenetic regulation Developmental reversion and methylation Epigenetic regulation is central to PH pathogenesis, often involving the pathological reactivation of transcriptional programs that are normally active only during fetal lung development [ ]. This hypothesis is supported by evidence from neonatal PH models demonstrating a persistent “fetal-like” pattern of tropoelastin gene expression [ ]. DNA methylation modulates this landscape through a dynamic interplay of enzymes. DNMT3B has been identified as a protective mediator [ ]. The transcriptional regulator SIN3a maintains BMPR2 expression by recruiting TET1 to prevent promoter hypermethylation, and its deficiency in PH leads to epigenetic silencing of BMPR2 and disease progression [ ]. Similarly, germline mutations and ubiquitous downregulation of TET2 occur in PH, leading to DNA hypermethylation and a pro-inflammatory phenotype driven by IL-1β that promotes vascular remodeling [ ]. Histone modifications Histone modification is a critical driver of proliferation. ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) upregulation drives pathological vascular remodeling in pulmonary and systemic circulation by fueling lipid synthesis and mediating GCN5-dependent histone acetylation to activate the pro-proliferative transcription factor FOXM1 [ ]. Similarly, nuclear SPHK2, activated by endothelial-derived EMAP II, generates sphingosine-1-phosphate to inhibit HDAC activity and increase histone H3K9 acetylation, thereby epigenetically activating a proliferative transcriptional program in SMCs [ ]. Histone methylation is also involved. ASH2L deficiency impairs KLF5 degradation, activating NOTCH3 signaling [ ]. Transcriptional co-activators like MED1 [ ] and Wnt signaling effectors FOSL1/2 [ ] further coordinate these remodeling programs. Non-coding RNAs Non-coding RNAs exert potent regulatory effects in PH [ ]. For example, in pediatric PAH associated with congenital heart disease (CHD-PAH), miR-27b is upregulated and suppresses the NOTCH1 pathway [ ], while long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) VELRP mediates proliferation in PASMCs [ ]. In adults, lncRNA H19 drives RV failure and serves as a specific biomarker for PH severity [ ]. Super-enhancer-driven lncRNAs are particularly active. UNC5B-AS1 promotes histone lactylation [ ], HCG20 activates the NLRP3 inflammasome [ ], and LINC00599 facilitates liquid-liquid phase separation [ ]. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) also play a role in pathogenesis and have translational value. Circ-GSAP suppresses SMAD4, serving as a prognostic biomarker for IPAH [ ], circ-Calm4 promotes pyroptosis [ ], and CircKrt4 induces endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) [ ]. Finally, sex-specific epigenetic mechanisms involving the Y-chromosome gene Uty [ ], ] and the lncRNA Xist [ ], ] contribute to the gender dimorphism observed in PH. RNA modifications RNA modifications drive pathology in PASMCs. Key mechanisms include m 6 A RNA modification via the Ythdf2/Myadm/p21 pathway [ ] and the YTHDF1-mediated translation of MAGED1 [ ]. Other modifications include ADAR1-mediated editing of circCDK17, which prevents degradation and leads to the accumulation of this circular RNA that drives SMC proliferation [ ]. Post-transcriptional and post-translational regulation At the post-transcriptional level, upregulation of the RNA-binding protein HNRNPA2B1 in PASMCs coordinates a pro-proliferative, anti-apoptotic phenotype, acting as a master regulator of phenotypic switching [ ]. Downstream at the protein level, post-translational modifications determine cell fate. The deubiquitinase USP15 prevents the ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation of YAP1 and TAZ, thereby sustaining SMC proliferation [ ]. Similarly, activation of the Hippo-TAZ-RUNX2 pathway drives vascular calcification and remodeling through the stabilization of the osteogenic factor RUNX2. Conversely, these mechanisms also regulate protective pathways. BRCC3 maintains pulmonary vascular homeostasis by deubiquitinating and stabilizing ALK2, which sustains protective BMP signaling while suppressing proliferative TGF-β signaling in SMCs [ ]. Metabolism and bioenergetic abnormalities Glucose metabolism and proliferative reprogramming PH is increasingly recognized as a “cancer-like” disease driven by profound metabolic reprogramming, often termed the Warburg effect ( ). Dysregulated polyamine metabolism acts as a critical metabolic switch similar to this effect, driving the proliferation of pulmonary vascular cells [ ]. Elevated plasma spermine levels are linked to greater clinical severity in PAH. Moreover, spermine has been shown to directly promote the proliferation of PASMCs in vitro , and inhibition of spermine synthase effectively attenuates PH in vivo [ ]. This proliferative drive is supported by specific enzymatic checkpoints. Inactivation of Malic Enzyme 1 in ECs alleviates PH by modulating the link between glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle [ ]. Similarly, the metabolic enzyme ALDH1A3 epigenetically activates the NFYA transcription factor to drive SMC proliferation and glycolysis [ ], while hypoxia triggers high levels of ENO1 in PAECs, activating the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway to promote metabolic reprogramming and remodeling [ ]. Furthermore, upregulation of fatty acid-binding proteins FABP4 and FABP5 in pulmonary ECs drives pathogenic glycolysis and distal arterialization, promoting severe PH and RV failure [ ]. Nucleotide metabolism is also hijacked. High levels of ATIC drive purine production, fueling PASMC hyperproliferation [ ]. Notably, this metabolic pattern is also context-dependent. Lipid and amino acid metabolism Dysregulation extends beyond glucose to lipid and amino acid pathways ( ). Comprehensive profiling identifies specific pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, such as 12,13-EpOME, associated with PH, while omega-3 derivatives like 8(9)-EpETE are linked to lower disease risk [ ]. Disrupted lipid signaling also interferes with therapeutic efficacy; dietary intake of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) counteracts statins in PH by restoring RhoA/ROCK2 signaling [ ]. Likewise, a high-soluble-fiber diet attenuates PH indirectly by modulating the gut microbiome to increase short-chain fatty acid production, thereby suppressing pulmonary vascular remodeling [ ]. Amino acid sensing is equally critical for remodeling. Activation of the GCN2 amino acid-sensing kinase mediates vascular remodeling [ ], while mechanical stress activates YAP/TAZ signaling to reprogram glutamine and serine metabolism in fibroblasts, fueling collagen biosynthesis and vascular stiffness [ ]. Additionally, increased IDO-1 expression drives systemic kynurenine pathway activation and de novo NAD + synthesis, promoting PH remodeling [ ]. Mitochondrial dynamics and function Mitochondrial dysfunction involves defects in fission, fusion, and quality control ( ). Excessive mitochondrial fission is driven by the Drp1 GTPase, and specific inhibition of Drp1 has shown efficacy in mitigating this process in both human PASMCs and animal models [ ]. Endothelial stability is further compromised by impaired mitophagy, a process governed by FUNDC1 [ ], and by loss of the deSUMOylase SENP1, which leads to hyper-SUMOylation of FIS1 and excessive fragmentation [ ]. Dysregulated post-translational modifications further disrupt mitochondrial quality control. SMYD2-mediated lysine methylation of PPARγ facilitates hypoxia-induced PH by aberrantly activating mitophagy [ ]. Biogenesis and enzymatic function are also impaired by specific deficiencies. Loss of NFU1 disrupts lipoic acid availability and angiogenesis [ ], while deficiency of Frataxin (FXN) triggers DNA damage and endothelial senescence [ ]. Similarly, endothelial deficiency of RAB7 impairs autophagic flux and mitochondrial function [ ]. Conversely, endothelial PGC-1α induction is essential for adaptive angiogenesis during hypoxic stress, and its failure leads to capillary rarefaction [ ]. Pathologically, endothelial upregulation of DKK1 activates the AKT/Sp1 axis to increase SHMT2, maintaining mitochondrial redox homeostasis to support proliferation [ ]. Oxidative stress and redox signaling Redox imbalance and specific signaling axes act as potent drivers of dysfunction ( ). Oxidative inactivation of the SERCA2 calcium pump drives remodeling by triggering the IRE1α/XBP1s endoplasmic reticulum stress pathway [ ]. Similarly, endothelial PHD2 deficiency suppresses Caveolin-1, leading to eNOS uncoupling and pathogenic nitrative stress [ ]. Additionally, a novel oxidative disulfide bond between Cyclin D and CDK4 normally acts as a brake on proliferation, but its deficiency in PH leads to unchecked CDK4 activity [ ]. Conversely, endogenous hydrogen sulfide exerts a protective effect. It inhibits PASMCs proliferation and vascular remodeling by persulfidating the endothelin type A receptor at Cysteine 69, preventing endothelin-1 binding [ ]. In the RV, mitochondrial oxidative stress mediates the transition to maladaptive failure [ ], driven partly by the reverse operation of the enzyme NNT [ ]. Programmed cell death and senescence Emerging programmed cell death and senescence mechanisms add complexity to the metabolic landscape ( ). Cathepsin L-induced degradation of BMPR2 triggers caspase-3/GSDME-dependent pyroptosis in pulmonary ECs [ ]. Metabolic dysfunction in PASMCs can trigger ferroptosis-mediated inflammation, which paradoxically promotes proliferation [ ]. This is regulated by factors like the circular RNA ca-circSCN8A , which promotes ferroptosis by recruiting EP300 to stabilize an R-loop that represses the antioxidant gene SLC7A11 [ ]. Regarding cell fate, contrary to expectation, the elimination of senescent cells exacerbates PH, suggesting a protective role for endothelial senescence in this context [ ]. Bioactive molecules Bioactive lipid mediators exert divergent effects on pulmonary vascular remodeling depending on the specific receptor subtype involved ( ). The prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) receptor DP1 serves a protective role by activating PKA to phosphorylate Raptor, thereby inhibiting pathogenic mTORC1-driven SMC proliferation [ ]. In contrast, the prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) receptor EP4 drives disease progression. It activates the cAMP/PKA pathway to enhance ANXA2 translation and phosphorylation, promoting β-catenin-dependent proliferation and PASMC reprogramming [ ]. Furthermore, EP4 activation in vascular SMCs promotes neointimal hyperplasia by stimulating the cAMP/PKA/mTORC1/rpS6 signaling axis to enhance the translation of Tenascin C [ ]. Estrogen plays a paradoxical role in PH metabolism as well. It upregulates the METTL3/PFKFB3 axis to drive vascular remodeling under normoxia, while on the other hand, it downregulates this axis via HIF-1α interference to confer protection under hypoxic conditions [ ]. Furthermore, estrogen promotes adaptive RV remodeling and prevents capillary rarefaction through a cardiomyocyte GC1-dependent pathway that stimulates VEGF-mediated angiogenesis [ ]. Inflammation and immune response Inflammation in PH often originates from endothelial injury and dysregulated signaling. For example, hypoxia-induced upregulation of endothelial NEDD9 promotes pathogenic platelet-endothelial adhesion, driving pulmonary vascular thrombosis and remodeling [ ]. Similarly, the downregulation of AREG and its receptor EGFR in pulmonary ECs triggers inflammation [ ]. Furthermore, a recent study indicates that deficiency of the lysosomal regulator NCOA7 leads to lysosomal acidification defects and the accumulation of inflammatory oxysterols, thereby promoting endothelial immunoactivation [ ]. Broader cytokine signaling also contributes to this environment, as IL-11 and IL-11Rα are more highly expressed in the pulmonary arteries of patients with IPAH and contribute to pulmonary artery remodeling [ ]. Additionally, PH induces neuroinflammation in the thoracic spinal cord, which drives sympathetic hyperactivity and RV failure [ ]. Monocytes Monocytes drive remodeling through distinct phenotypes and recruitment pathways. Single-cell transcriptomics reveals that high-altitude pulmonary hypertension (HAPH) is characterized by an expansion of intermediate and non-classical monocytes with downregulated HIF-1α and a distinct inflammatory phenotype [ ]. These cells are often recruited by resident populations. Hypoxia-induced proliferation of resident interstitial macrophages promotes the recruitment of CCR2 + monocytes via CCL2, which subsequently release thrombospondin-1 to activate TGF-β and drive remodeling, a pathway which could be inhibited by dexamethasone [ ]. Complementing these findings, therapeutic modulation of the splenic neuroimmune pathway through ultrasound was shown to downregulate the activation of monocytes and macrophages, improving experimental PH [ ]. Macrophages Macrophages are central effectors in PH, acting on specific vascular targets. Macrophages directly promote medial thickening. A unique population of interstitial macrophages characterized as MHCII hi LYVE1 lo CCR2 hi infiltrates the medial layer, driving fibrosis by activating the Wnt11-planar cell polarity pathway in SMCs [ ]. Additionally, Caspase-8 in macrophages drives PH by activating the NLRP3 inflammasome to release IL-1β, which further stimulates SMC proliferation [ ]. Consistent with this, myeloid cell-derived IL-1β drives pulmonary vascular remodeling and right heart dysfunction in a murine model of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [ ]. In addition, activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in CCR2 + macrophages infiltrating the RV tissue drives cardiac inflammation and fibrosis, contributing to RV failure [ ]. Macrophages also disrupt endothelial homeostasis. In obesity-related HFpEF, metabolic stress activates the c-Fos/Dusp1 pathway in alveolar macrophages, driving pyroptosis and inflammation that causes paracrine endothelial damage [ ]. Furthermore, STING signaling promotes PH through a non-interferon-dependent mechanism involving the regulation of VEGF secretion from myeloid cells, driving endothelial apoptosis and remodeling [ ]. Recent studies have identified the role of gut and airway microbiota in PH [ ]. The gut microbial metabolite TMAO promotes inflammation by stimulating macrophages to release proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines [ ]. Conversely, a high-soluble-fiber diet attenuates PH by modulating the gut microbiome to increase short-chain fatty acid production, which in turn suppresses pulmonary vascular inflammation and remodeling [ ]. Several pathways highlight the protective or regulatory potential of macrophages [ ], ]. Regnase-1 acts as a negative regulator by degrading Il6 and Pdgf mRNAs in alveolar macrophages, preventing cytokine overproduction [ ]. Similarly, the macrophage-specific Peli1–Foxp1–IL-6 axis has been identified as a key regulator, where Peli1 deficiency reduces IL-6-mediated inflammation [ ]. Therapeutically, adoptive transfer of immunoregulatory macrophages with an M2reg phenotype has been shown to suppress monocyte recruitment and restore immune functionality [ ]. Granulocytes Neutrophil-derived S100A9 activates the RAGE/PI3K/AKT signaling axis in pulmonary ECs, driving endothelial dysfunction and vascular remodeling [ ]. Reactivation of HERV-K in neutrophils drives an antiviral-like immune response characterized by excessive elastase release, which promotes remodeling [ ]. Furthermore, a single-cell atlas of peripheral neutrophils identified a cluster characterized by high MMP9 expression that independently predicts mortality in IPAH [ ]. In contrast to the pathogenic role of neutrophils, eosinophils exert a protective role by releasing the ALOX15-derived lipid mediators 14-HDHA and 17-HDHA, which suppress perivascular inflammation and inhibit SMC proliferation via PPARγ activation [ ]. T cells and NK cells Dysregulation of T cells and NK cells influences remodeling through interactions with ECs and SMCs as well. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) attenuate pulmonary venous remodeling in PH-LHD by employing NLRC3 to suppress IL-18 secretion, thereby inhibiting pathogenic EndMT [ ]. Clinically, a “TRGscore” based on Treg-related hub genes accurately distinguishes PAH patients from controls [ ]. Deletion of the oxygen sensor PHD2 in CD8 + T cells stabilizes HIF-1α, driving a glycolytic switch and excessive cytokine production that exacerbates cardiac inflammation and pulmonary vascular remodeling [ ]. Spatial single-cell imaging further maps immune dysregulation, identifying TIM-3 + T cells and IDO-1 + TIM-3 + SAMHD1 + dendritic cells (DCs) as contributors to PH progression [ ]. While inhibition of Th17 cells by donepezil ameliorates lung fibrosis and PH [ ], adaptive checkpoints show context-dependent effects. For instance, PD-1/PD-L1 signaling triggers hypoxia-induced remodeling by suppressing Th17-associated inflammation via the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway [ ]. Additionally, recent single-cell data demonstrates that TCF7-driven activation of stressed NK cells regulates the secretion of SPP1, driving the proliferation and migration of PASMCs [ ]. B cells, autoimmunity and complement system Autoimmune mechanisms and the complement system further exacerbate vascular inflammation. Autoimmunity is a significant feature of IPAH, where pathogenic autoantibodies target ECs and correlate with disease severity [ ]. This autoimmunity is underpinned by B cell dysregulation. Unsupervised transcriptomic profiling of whole blood identifies a distinct subgroup of IPAH patients with poor survival, characterized by B cell lymphopenia and the downregulation of genes involved in B cell receptor signaling and immunoglobulin production. Recognition of this distinct molecular endotype provides an opportunity for early risk stratification [ ]. In the context of systemic sclerosis (SSc), elevated levels of soluble B cell activation markers, particularly BAFF and sBCMA, distinguish SSc patients with PH from those without, implicating dysregulated B cell immunity in the pathogenesis of SSc vasculopathy [ ]. Specific immunoglobulin isotypes also drive distinct pathways. For example, elevated serum IgE promotes pulmonary vascular remodeling by activating mast cells via the FcεRIα receptor to release IL-6 and IL-13. Thus, targeting the IgE-FcεRI axis represents a novel method for PH treatment [ ]. These responses can be triggered by innate sensors. Chronic activation of TLR7/8 in the presence of endothelial injury triggers a fulminant autoimmune response characterized by autoantibody production and perivascular inflammation [ ]. Immunoglobulin accumulation, particularly IgG, activates the alternative complement pathway, which stimulates GM-CSF production to drive perivascular inflammation [ ]. Additionally, intracellular activation of the complement system (Factor D) reprograms pulmonary artery fibroblasts toward a glycolytic and proinflammatory phenotype, highlighting the potential of complement-targeted interventions to reverse metabolic reprogramming and attenuate inflammation in PH [ ]. Finally, decreased galactosylation of plasma IgG N-glycans characterizes a proinflammatory phenotype in CTEPH, establishing the IgG N-glycome as a potential driver of vascular inflammation [ ]. Taken together, the immune landscape of PH can be organized into a coordinated immunoregulatory framework ( ). Innate immune cells, including macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, and NK cells, act as early sensors and amplifiers of vascular injury by producing proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines that promote endothelial dysfunction and SMC proliferation, and recruit adaptive immune cells. Adaptive immune cells, particularly dysregulated T-cell subsets and B cells, sustain chronic inflammation through cytokine release and autoantibody production, reinforcing vascular remodeling. These immune cell populations collectively maintain perivascular inflammation and maladaptive remodeling, thereby driving PH progression. Mechanical stress and mechanosensation Mechanotransduction and shear stress Mechanical stress is a potent regulator of pulmonary vascular cell fate, sensed primarily through specialized ion channels and transcription factors. The mechanosensitive channel Piezo1 is upregulated in pulmonary ECs during PH, where it translates mechanical stretch into pathogenic Notch signaling via the Ca 2+ /AKT/Jagged1 axis, driving vascular remodeling [ ]. In SMCs, Piezo1 also drives excessive proliferation and vasoconstriction via calcium influx, while paradoxically preventing endothelial senescence in hypoxia-induced PH [ ]. In contrast, the mechanosensitive iron channel Piezo2 plays a protective homeostatic role; its endothelial deficiency impairs intracellular calcium signaling and angiogenesis, thereby promoting pulmonary vascular rarefaction [ ]. Beyond ion channels, shear stress directly modulates transcriptional programs. Pathological high shear stress suppresses the transcription factor ERG in lung ECs, causing EndMT and driving progressive PH [ ].

Upregulation of the store-operated calcium channel protein Orai1 drives pathogenic calcium influx, proliferation, and vasoconstriction in PASMCs [ ]. Research further identifies Calcium Sensing Receptor (CaSR) overactivation, driven by gain-of-function variants and hypoxia-induced self-polymerization, as a critical pathogenic mechanism in PH. Targeting CaSR via polymerization-blocking peptides or Au-modified ceria nanozymes effectively mitigates intracellular calcium overload and vascular remodeling, validating CaSR as a promising therapeutic target [ ], [ ], [ ]. Extracellular matrix (ECM) and structural remodeling Hemodynamic forces drive profound structural changes in the vessel wall. Degradation of arterial elastin by elastases drives pulmonary arterial stiffening and hypertension in left heart disease, identifying ECM remodeling as a therapeutic target [ ]. Similarly, loss of the ECM proteoglycan lumican in PASMCs promotes AKT-driven SMC proliferation [ ]. These structural changes are not limited to the arterial side; a porcine model of pulmonary venous hypertension reveals that mechanical stress drives distinct proteomic reprogramming in pulmonary veins, characterized by TGF-β-mediated EndMT [ ]. In the context of CTEPH, structural resolution is critical. Impairment of intrathrombus angiogenesis prevents clot resolution and promotes disease progression [ ]. Therapeutic strategies targeting these structural defects show promise. Restoration of FGF-10 signaling reverses established emphysema and PH by promoting lung regeneration [ ]. The hemodynamic burden of PH ultimately compromises the right ventricle. RV failure in human PH is driven by a biophysical defect where myosin heads are sequestered in a super-relaxed state, impairing thick filament activation and contractile reserve [ ]. To better understand these impairments, unsupervised cluster analysis of advanced hemodynamic parameters has identified five distinct RV functional subphenotypes, revealing unique profiles of diastolic stiffness and ventriculo-arterial coupling [ ]. Structurally, advanced 3D deep tissue imaging has revealed that the microvascular architecture of the failing RV undergoes complex adaptive remodeling rather than simple capillary rarefaction [ ]. Our recent study underscores the role of AXL in driving PH RV remodeling through its orchestration of the ECM [ ]. Biomarkers BMP/TGF-β signaling and metabolic stress Metabolic dysregulation and hemodynamic stress leave distinct footprints in the circulation. High levels of serum uric acid (UA) are a strong predictor of poor survival, although UA is considered a byproduct of metabolic stress in the lung rather than a causal driver of the disease [ ]. Similarly, right atrial dilatation and pressure overload in pre-capillary PH trigger increased expression and secretion of BMP10 from the right atrium, establishing circulating BMP10 as a dynamic biomarker of right heart strain that is reversible upon hemodynamic unloading [ ]. Additionally, high serum levels of the TGF-β superfamily members activin A and follistatin-like 3 (FSTL3) serve as strong prognostic biomarkers for PH [ ]. Dual role as biomarker and therapeutic targets Beyond passive markers, proteomic profiling identifies proteins that actively drive or resolve pathology. Large-scale proteogenomic profiling identifies netrin-4 and thrombospondin-2 as causal determinants of PAH, with netrin-4 driving adverse outcomes and thrombospondin-2 providing protective effects via ECM regulation [ ]. Some biomarkers also represent viable therapeutic targets. For instance, SUR1 induces pulmonary vasodilation and reverses vascular remodeling, establishing it as a dual biomarker and target [ ]. Furthermore, ErbB3 modulates hypoxia-induced endothelial dysfunction and may serve as a marker to predict disease activity [ ]. Inflammatory and immune biomarkers Inflammatory cytokines and immune checkpoint molecules provide critical prognostic information. Elevated levels of TRAIL and MIF, alongside reduced CCL5 and CX3CL1, independently predict mortality in PH [ ]. More specific immune pathways are also implicated; the immune checkpoint receptor ACKR4 is reduced in PAH and correlates with disease progression [ ]. Furthermore, circulating HMGB2 promotes PASMC proliferation through RAGE/FAK–Hippo/YAP signaling, with higher serum levels predicting mortality [ ]. Integration of metabolomics and transcriptomics identified six hypoxia-induced metabolism-associated hub genes ( Cat , Ephx1 , Gpx3 , Gstm4 , Gstm5 , and Gsto1 ) as diagnostic biomarkers [ ]. Platelets exhibit a distinct RNA profile characterized by upregulation of mitochondrial and translational pathways, serving as a non-invasive diagnostic tool [ ]. Special progress in pediatric PH Pediatric PH exhibits distinct genetic, metabolic, hemodynamic, and clinical characteristics that differentiate it fundamentally from adult-onset PH ( ). Genetic landscape of pediatric PH The genetic landscape of pediatric PH is notably distinct from adult PH ( ). While BMPR2 is the most common genetic cause of PH in general [ ], early studies noted a conspicuous absence of BMPR2 mutations in pediatric cohorts, suggesting a different genetic basis [ ]. Recent whole-exome sequencing confirmed this distinction, revealing that pediatric-onset PAH carries a significantly greater overall genetic burden than adult disease [ ]. This unique landscape is defined by the enrichment of specific mutations. Unlike in adults, variants in TBX4 are significantly enriched in children with IPAH [ ], ], causing a spectrum of lung disorders [ ]. In pediatric patients, the genetic profile of CHD-PAH is distinct from that of IPAH. Notably, among the 12 definitive PAH-causing genes ( BMPR2 , EIF2AK4 , ACVRL1 , ENG , CAV1 , KCNK3 , TBX4 , SOX17 , SMAD9 , ATP13A3 , GDF2 and KDR ), while BMPR2 mutations predominate in both types, the secondary mutation patterns differ, with ACVRL1 being second most common in IPAH and SOX17 / TBX4 more prevalent in CHD-PAH [ ]. This is to some extent consistent with another study featuring SOX17 as CHD-PAH candidate risk gene, explaining up to 3.2 % of the cases [ ]. Other key genes including ACVRL1 and EIF2AK4 have also been identified as significant contributors in pediatric PH cohorts [ ]. These mutations have direct clinical implications. ACVRL1 mutations are associated with an earlier age of onset and more severe hemodynamics in children [ ], as mutations in ENG and ACVRL1 impair Smad signaling to drive proliferation [ ]. Additionally, loss-of-function mutations in the KCNK3 potassium channel define a novel channelopathy that drives PASMC proliferation by altering membrane potential [ ]. Development-related metabolism in children Pediatric PH presents distinct metabolic and developmental characteristics. In persistent PH of the newborn (PPHN), the metabolic shift manifests as decreased eNOS expression, which impairs mitochondrial biogenesis and elevates oxidative stress [ ]. Neonatal PASMC proliferation is uniquely regulated by nitric oxide (NO) [ ], and PPHN is associated with increased expression of VEGF and its receptor Flt-1 [ ]. Developmentally, neonatal hyperoxia downregulates endothelial Cpt1a expression, leading to impaired fatty acid oxidation and pathogenic EndMT [ ]. Elder children with CHD-PAH show systemic disturbances, including significant alterations in the lung microbiome, characterized by enrichment of Streptococcus and Rothia [ ] and a disturbed metabolome profile, particularly in purine and glycerophospholipid pathways [ ]. A critical aspect in this population is the role of endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs); EPC levels are inversely correlated with PAH severity in children with CHD [ ], and therapies such as treprostinil have been shown to increase EPC counts and boost their angiogenic capacity [ ]. Pediatric hemodynamics and developmental models Unlike adults, children often experience aberrant flow and pressure patterns due to congenital structural anomalies or early postnatal adaptations. Clinically, the RV systolic-to-diastolic duration ratio (S:D ratio) has been reported as a pediatric-specific echocardiographic biomarker, with each 0.1 increase predicting a 13 % rise in annual mortality or transplantation risk [ ]. Mechanistically, neonatal models of Right Ventricular Outflow Tract (RVOT) obstruction by pulmonary artery or vein banding reproduce developmental RV pressure overload and disturbed pulmonary perfusion, driving cardiomyocyte proliferation, vascular remodeling, and pulmonary dysplasia [ ], [ ], [ ]. These pathological alterations closely resemble pediatric pathophysiology. Therapeutic interventions in this context are also being explored. For instance, a novel neonatal rat model of pulmonary vein stenosis demonstrates that the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus effectively suppresses neointimal hyperplasia and preserves vessel patency [ ]. In children with CHD-PAH, serum endostatin levels correlate with disease severity and transplant-free survival [ ]. Novel mechanistic markers are also being validated. THBS4 is markedly upregulated in plasma and PASMCs, mirroring disease severity in children [ ], while NEK2 drives proliferation via NF-κB, suggesting utility as both a biomarker and therapeutic target [ ]. Additionally, distinct trans -right-ventricle and transpulmonary microRNA gradients have been identified in children, correlating with cardiac remodeling [ ]. Recognition of pediatric-specific mechanisms of PH emphasizes the importance of targeted diagnostic strategies and clinical management for children. While exploring the complex pathogenesis is crucial for our understanding of PH, the next vital step is to translate these insights into clinical practice to ultimately improve patients’ outcome. Advances in genetics, metabolism, immune regulation and biomechanical forces are now guiding this transition, helping to identify new diagnostic strategies, risk stratification models, pharmacotherapy, and interventional methods. The following sections review how these mechanistic discoveries are integrated into modern clinical management paradigms of PH. Progress in PAH clinical management Clinical diagnosis and risk-based treatment strategies Diagnostic approach The 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines formalized a lower hemodynamic threshold for PH (mPAP>20 mmHg) and emphasized PVR ≥2–3 WU plus pulmonary arterial wedge pressure (PAWP) ≤15 mmHg to define PAH, while codifying a three-step pathway: suspicion (primary care), detection (echo/NT-proBNP), and confirmation with right heart catheterization (RHC) in expert centers [ ]. The guidelines also highlight systematic screening in high-risk groups (CTD, CHD, heritable forms) and a tighter integration of cardiopulmonary exercise testing, V/Q scanning and Cardiac MRI (CMR) into work-up. Risk assessment has become the central organizing principle of management. The REVEAL Lite 2 score, using seven non-invasive variables, was developed and validated as a practical alternative to full REVEAL 2.0 while retaining excellent discrimination for 1-year mortality [ ]. Subsequent work comparing and validating risk tools shows that REVEAL Lite 2 and modern ESC/ERS 3-strata/4-strata models both identify higher risk strata with stepwise worsening survival and are sensitive to changes over time, supporting a treat-to-target strategy rather than “set and forget” therapy [ ]. In practice, contemporary algorithms combine: 1) Baseline multiparametric risk assessment (WHO FC, 6-min walk distance (6MWD)/cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), biomarkers, RV imaging, hemodynamics). 2) Early re-assessment at 3–6 months after therapy initiation or escalation. 3) Therapeutic decisions anchored to achieving and maintaining low-risk status, with explicit thresholds for escalation as codified in ESC/ERS and the new ERJ treatment algorithm [ ]. Evolving treatment paradigm The last five years have consolidated the shift from step-wise monotherapy to early combination therapy: The ERS 2024 treatment algorithm recommends initial dual oral combination (ERA + PDE5i/sGC stimulator) for most newly diagnosed low- and intermediate-risk patients and parenteral prostacyclin-based combinations (often triple therapy) for high-risk disease [ ]. In addition, a focused review of upfront combination therapy summarized randomized and observational data (including AMBITION and subsequent trials), concluding that early combination reduces clinical failure vs. monotherapy, especially in younger, lower-comorbidity cohorts [ ]. More recent reviews emphasize tailoring therapy to comorbidities (older, cardiometabolic phenotypes), and integrating new pathways such as activin/BMP inhibition into risk-based algorithms [ ]. Despite this, contemporary real-world registries still show substantial under-use of combination and parenteral therapy, underscoring the gap between guidelines and practice – an important theme for a critical review. Drug development: beyond pure vasodilation Expansion from 3 to 4 therapeutic pathways Traditional PAH therapies target three signaling pathways (endothelin, NO, prostacyclin). The updated ERJ algorithm explicitly adds a fourth pathway, BMPR2/activin signaling, reflecting the emergence of sotatercept [ ], ]. Sotatercept (activin ligand trap) In the phase 2 PULSAR trial, sotatercept on top of background therapy significantly reduced PVR and improved 6MWD and NT-proBNP compared with placebo, in a population already receiving 1–3 PAH drugs [ ]. The phase 3 STELLAR trial confirmed robust improvements in 6MWD and a composite of clinical worsening, with consistent benefits across subgroups and hints of vascular “reverse remodeling” (e.g., improved WHO FC, hemodynamics) [ ]. Recent pipeline reviews position sotatercept as the prototype of pathobiology-modifying therapy [ ]. To further define its role across the clinical spectrum, trials such as HYPERION and ZENITH are currently evaluating its efficacy in newly diagnosed patients and higher-risk cohorts [ ], ].
